item.itunes:summary:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mr-ZRGHP74I

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析威權體制下的「政績合法性契約」，理解經濟下行如何動搖執政根基。
  • 破除「經濟變差政權便立即崩潰」的簡化迷思，從歷史脈絡與制度層面客觀審視政權轉型的關鍵門檻。
  • 揭示中國房地產與地方財政深度綁定的結構性困局，精準指出財政危機轉化為政權危機的連鎖反應。

摘要

經濟困境不等於政權崩潰：燃料與火花的本質區別

作者指出，每當官方經濟數據疲軟時，輿論常迅速興起「政權即將崩潰」的論調。然而回顧歷史，無論是過去嚴重的飢荒、文化大革命，或是北韓的極端困境，威權體制在深重災難中依然能夠延續。作者強調，經濟危機通常只是「燃料」，而非直接點燃體制崩解的「火花」。單純的經濟衰退並不足以撼動統治，唯有當危機蔓延至財政體系、引發深刻社會矛盾與體制內部撕裂，甚至波及軍警等國家暴力機器運作時，經濟問題才會真正轉化為威脅統治根基的政治危機。

經濟引擎失速：從高速狂飆轉向長期放緩

檢視當前經濟數據，作者認為中國並非瞬間撞牆倒下，而是正在經歷長期放緩的結構性轉折。過去支撐高速發展的六大支柱——人口紅利、世界工廠式的出口、外資與技術引進、房地產開發、大規模基礎建設及地方舉債模式，如今已逐漸達到邊際效應極限。當前房地產銷售滑落、內需消費疲軟與人口高齡化等現象並存，過往依靠兩位數高增長來掩蓋與消化債務的循環已難以維持，驅動經濟前進的舊引擎已面臨熄火挑戰。

地方財政危機與「威權契約」的瓦解風險

作者特別提醒，評估政權穩定度不能僅看GDP數值，核心在於「政府手中是否有充裕的資金」。在中國，房地產不僅是單一產業，更是與地方政府財政（土地財政）緊密相連的命脈。房市低迷導致土地出讓收入萎縮，但龐大的存量債務依然存在。若危機進一步導致基層公務員欠薪、公共服務停滯，甚至基層行政與維穩資源匱乏，便意味著經濟問題已開始侵蝕國家機器本身。作者總結，體制與大眾之間存在著「政績合法性」或「威權契約」——即民眾默許政治權利的讓渡，換取生活品質年年提升；一旦改善生活的承諾破滅且發展紅利耗盡，政權維繫民心的根本依據將面臨前所未有的考驗。

================================================

Let house prices fall further, let unemployment rise, the sooner the economy collapses, the sooner the CCP will fall. >> Economic deterioration does increase pressure, but can it truly lead to a regime transition? In political science, this exchange under an authoritarian system is called a "performance-based legitimacy" contract. People accept limited political participation, while the regime trades economic performance, security, and benefits for stability. But this exchange has a major prerequisite. Life must truly keep getting better. If it starts to become a reality where house prices keep dropping, wages stagnate, college graduates can't find ideal jobs, business becomes harder, and the next generation feels they can't possibly be wealthier than their parents , then people will start asking: You told me we couldn't do without the Communist Party because it could develop China. But if development slows down today, what does the CCP have left to maintain the hearts and minds of the people? People often ask about the map in my background. This map isn't just my dream. for the territory of the Republic of China; it’s what the Republic of China should look like in the eyes of all 1.4 billion Chinese descendants. We aim to restore the Republic of China, using the Three Principles of the People from the National Revolution to fulfill the mission of reclaiming the Republic and rebuilding the nation. We have launched a product bundle featuring map posters, tapestries, throw pillows, and ROC flag keychains. Why choose? Get them all for just 1911. Also, on both platforms, orders over 699 get free shipping. Friends overseas don't worry, we will launch international purchasing options soon, so hurry up and grab yours! >> Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. Over the past few years, whenever the CCP official. releases lackluster economic figures, the internet immediately erupts with " The CCP is about to collapse!" Real estate falls, the CCP is about to collapse! Youth can't find jobs, the CCP is about to collapse! Local governments in debt, the CCP is about to collapse! Consumption is weak, the CCP is about to collapse. Sometimes, even if the A-shares drop for a few days, people start calculating, "At this speed, does the CCP only have three years left?" The question is, will an authoritarian regime really collapse just because the economy is bad? If it were that simple, the CCP would have collapsed countless times already. In the past, the mainland experienced economic and food disasters far worse than today, yet the CCP didn't collapse . The Cultural Revolution turned Chinese society upside down, yet the CCP didn't collapse. North Korea went through severe famine, yet the Kim regime didn't collapse. There are many authoritarian governments worldwide that have survived for years despite severe economic crises. So today, the real question we should be. asking isn't whether China's economy will keep getting worse, but rather how bad it has to get before it turns into a political crisis that truly shakes the CCP's grip on power? These two things are completely different. I’ll give you the most important answer upfront: an economic crisis is fuel, but it’s usually not the spark that topples an authoritarian regime. The real danger arises when an economic crisis spirals into a fiscal crisis, a social crisis, and infighting within the Party, eventually causing issues even within the military and. police—the coercive apparatus that maintains the regime. Only when it reaches that point can an economic collapse potentially lead to political collapse. Before we rush to wait for the CCP to fall, let's look at how bad the Chinese economy actually is right now. In the first half of 2026, the official GDP growth announced by the CCP was 4.7%—5% in the first quarter, dropping to 4.3% in the second. For many mature economies, 4.7%is actually quite high, so if someone tells you that the Chinese economy has.

completely collapsed and will turn into the Soviet Union tomorrow, they are clearly jumping the gun. But if someone else tells you that because GDP is still at 4.7%, there are no problems at all with the Chinese economy, that is equally naive. Because the real problem for China today is not whether there is growth, but whether the engines that drove that high-speed growth in the past can still keep running. Let’s look at a few numbers: in the first seven months of 2026, total retail. sales of consumer goods in China grew by only 1.2%, with a mere 0.6%increase in July alone. The issues in real estate are even more apparent; in the first seven months of this year, sales of newly built commercial housing fell by 13.1%year-on-year, and funding for real estate developers dropped by 20.3%. On the other hand, Chinese exports still show considerable resilience, with official figures showing 14%growth in the first seven months of this year, while the national urban unemployment rate remains at around 5.2%. So, if I had to describe China today in one sentence: it hasn't hit a wall suddenly, but is experiencing a long-term slowdown. China used to be a car used to racing at 150 km/h; now it has slowed down to 80 or 90. The car is still moving and the engine hasn't stalled, but the trouble is that there might be a very long downhill slope ahead. What has China’s high-speed economic growth relied on since the Reform and Opening-up? Simply put, it’s a few things: First, the demographic dividend, with waves of. young people entering factories. Second , exports, as China became the world’s factory. Third, foreign capital and technology, with companies shifting supply chains to China. Fourth, real estate, where local governments sell land, developers build houses, banks issue loans, and families buy them. Fifth, infrastructure, with highways, high-speed rail, airports, and industrial parks being built rapidly. Sixth, local government debt, where they borrow to build, hoping future growth will digest the debt. The biggest feature of this entire model. is that as long as the economy keeps growing at a high speed, many problems can be masked by that growth. 110 billion might seem scary today, but if GDP grows by 10%next year and land prices rise, it doesn't seem like such a big problem anymore. But now the trouble has arrived: the population is aging, the real estate sector is declining, local governments are heavily in debt, household consumption is insufficient, and the marginal utility of investment is getting worse. In its 2024 assessment of China, the IMF also specifically pointed out that the ongoing real estate. adjustment, high debt, weak domestic demand, and factors related to population and productivity will all drag down China's medium-to-long-term growth potential. So the real question to ask now is no longer whether it’s 4.5%or 5%this year, but rather, if this formula that powered China for the last 40 years has truly reached its end, what will the CCP rely on to maintain its rule for the next 20 years? I think the point most people easily overlook is that when we look at China's. economy, we often just look at GDP. But if you want to judge whether a regime is in danger, I would look at whether the government itself has money , because for China, real estate isn't just a regular industry; it is tied to local government finances. In the past, a major source of revenue for many local governments was selling land: developers bought land, borrowed from banks, built houses, and citizens bought them. Local governments collected land revenue and used it to build new roads, industrial parks, and subways. So when real estate was booming, everyone.

felt rich: local governments had money, developers had money, banks felt secure , and homeowners felt their properties were becoming more valuable year by year . But what about now? Houses are hard to sell, developers don't dare to acquire land, and local land revenue is falling . However, the debt borrowed previously won't disappear just because housing prices dropped, so local governments are now facing a very troublesome question: where will the money come from? This is why the IMF keeps emphasizing that China's local government and local. financing platform debts need further handling. When will this issue turn from economic news into political news? If a locality builds one less stadium, the CCP won't collapse; if they hold one less fireworks show, it won't either. But if one day a large number of regions start delaying civil servant salaries, slashing teacher compensation, facing problems with healthcare and social security, defaulting on payments to private enterprises, seeing public service quality decline, or even having basic administrative and police. operations affected by finances, then the nature of the situation changes. Because this means the economic crisis has begun to erode the state apparatus itself; that is why I have always believed that for the people it is a livelihood issue, but when the government runs out of money, it starts to become a regime issue. Since the reform and opening-up, the CCP has essentially formed an unwritten political bargain with many mainlanders , which can be summarized as: "You don't challenge my rule, and I will make your life better year by year." You cannot vote to replace the Communist Party, but your income increases, you can buy homes, cars, travel abroad, your children can go to college, and China's national strength grows day by day. So even if many people are dissatisfied with politics, they figure it's fine, as long as life is still improving. In political science, this type of exchange under an authoritarian system is called an "authoritarian contract," where the public accepts limited political participation, and the regime trades economic performance, security, and benefit distribution for legitimacy. . But there is one major prerequisite to this exchange: life must genuinely keep getting better. If property values start to plummet, wages stagnate, college graduates cannot find ideal jobs, doing business becomes increasingly difficult, and the next generation feels they will never be as wealthy as their parents, then people will begin to ask: "You told me we couldn't do without the Party because it ensures development, so if development slows down today, what does the CCP have left to maintain stability?" This doesn't mean the people will revolt , but it will slowly erode a crucial pillar of the CCP's legitimacy since the reform and opening-up. Let's first discuss: if people become poorer, will they really revolt? The answer is not necessarily; in fact, most of the time they won't. In democratic countries, if the economy is poor, the people have a clear exit: they can change the government. If a president fails, they step down in four years; if the ruling party ruins the economy, they switch to another party in the next election. But in a one-party. dictatorship, there is no such exit. So , what do the people do? Some choose to "lie flat," some decide not to have children, and some cut back on consumption. Others take civil service exams, try to emigrate, or complain online all day. But complaining and revolution are two entirely different things. Suppose there are 10 million people in the mainland today cursing the Communist Party at home, but they don't know each other, have no organization, no leaders , no funds, no media, and no cross-city connection. The political threat of those 10 million.

might be less than that of 100,000 people who are truly organized. Therefore, what an authoritarian regime fears most is not that the people are dissatisfied, but that they begin to organize. This is why the CCP is particularly sensitive toward independent labor unions, cross-regional social movements, independent media, and political organizations. Because when one person curses the government at home , it is just an emotion; but when a group of people begins to make demands together, that is politics. So, never assume that if China's economy is bad, the people will demand reform and the. CCP will be forced to democratize. History does not guarantee this path at all. There is another possibility: because the economy is poor, people are dissatisfied, and the regime feels society is unstable, it may then strengthen stability maintenance, tighten speech control, emphasize national security even more, and stress nationalism. Ultimately, instead of becoming democratic, it becomes more centralized. Furthermore, economic problems can be reinterpreted—why is China's economy poor? It is not that our policies have problems; it is that the United States is suppressing China, the. West is containing China, and foreign powers do not want the Chinese nation to rise. Therefore, we must not be in chaos now, and the people nationwide must unite even more closely around the Party Central Committee. This narrative is crucial for an authoritarian system because it can transform dissatisfaction with the government into anger toward external enemies. So, a very counter-intuitive conclusion is that economic decline sometimes does not lead to political opening, but may instead lead to even tougher political control. If we look back at the CCP's own history , it becomes very clear: during the. Great Leap Forward, the lives of mainland people were much more difficult than today. That was a truly massive humanitarian disaster, but the CCP did not fall. Why ? Because the Party remained, the military remained, the public security forces remained, and the local administrative systems remained. The people also lacked any independent organization that could span the entire country to replace the Communist Party. The Cultural Revolution was the same: the entire society suffered massive destruction, and China even fell into severe political chaos, but in the end,. the Communist Party still reclaimed order. Therefore, we must face a very cruel fact: if just economic downturns and the suffering of the masses were enough to topple the CCP, then the CCP would have already fallen in the 1960s. This is why political science research usually does not regard economic crisis as a single sufficient condition for the collapse of an authoritarian regime. Economic deterioration increases pressure, but whether it can truly cause a regime transition also depends on ruling elites, social organizations, and. the regime's control capabilities, among other things. When will an economic crisis truly turn into a political crisis? I believe we must look at at least a few conditions. The first is when cross-class dissatisfaction begins to converge. Normally, a young person who cannot find work only thinks it is a youth problem; a homeowner whose property value drops thinks it is a real estate problem; an entrepreneur who cannot make money thinks it is a business environment problem; a local civil servant who is unpaid thinks it is a local fiscal problem; and retirees worried about health insurance think it is a social security problem. But what is truly. dangerous is when these people suddenly start to feel that our problems are actually the same problem, and in the end, they all point to the same system. At this point, economic dissatisfaction will truly begin to be politicized. The second truly dangerous condition is when the Communist Party itself splits. I think this is even more important than how many people are protesting on the streets. An authoritarian regime is at its strongest not when no one dislikes it, but when the ruling elite is highly united, and everyone believes that staying with the regime is still in.

their best interest. However, the most troublesome aspect of an economic crisis is that the pie gets smaller. In the past, when the economy grew by 8%annually, the central government could get a share, local governments could get a share, state-owned enterprises could get a share; officials had political achievements, and entrepreneurs made money. Even if everyone was annoyed with each other, there was at least more and more food on the table. What if the economy stagnates today? Then the problem arises: who is going to swallow the losses? Local governments, the central government, state banks, private enterprises, the middle class, homeowners—who is ultimately going to. foot the bill for local debts? Research in political science on authoritarian systems also points out that elite unity is, in itself, an essential pillar of regime stability. And when economic performance worsens and the distribution of benefits becomes uncertain, some members of the ruling elite are more likely to consider abandoning the original regime coalition. Therefore, what could truly endanger the CCP is not just the public realizing they are broke , but the day when even people inside the Communist Party start to feel that " if we keep following this system, I will lose my money, my power, and perhaps. even my life." At this point, everyone starts looking for an exit. Some advocate for reform, some for changing leaders, some try to push the blame onto others, and some start secretly contacting external forces. Once it reaches this stage, an economic crisis truly becomes a crisis of power. The third condition is that opposition forces begin to organize. But intra-party strife alone is not enough; society must develop real organizational capabilities. For example, students, workers, the. middle class, local rights activists, intellectuals, and entrepreneurs— different groups must stop complaining in isolation and start forming common political demands. What is even more important is cross-city coordination. A protest of 1,000 people in Shanghai might not shake the central government, but if after something happens in Shanghai, Beijing responds, Guangzhou responds, Chengdu responds, and Wuhan responds, and they start to have common slogans, common leadership, and common political demands, the nature of the situation changes entirely because it is. no longer a mass incident, but a nationwide political movement. The fourth condition is whether those who hold the guns are still obedient. The final hurdle is usually the most realistic and cruel one: the military and the public security apparatus. 1989 is actually a very important example. At that time, there was inflation and corruption, demands for political reform , and large-scale student and citizen movements. Even the highest levels of the CCP had serious divisions on how to handle the movement. So you see, mass mobilization was there , social discontent was there, political demands were there, and a split at the top also occurred, but in the end, the CCP did not fall. Why? One critical reason is that the military ultimately continues to carry out the hardline policies of the center ; thus, for many authoritarian regimes, the true moment of collapse is not when people first take to the streets, but when the military and police first tell their top leader, "This time, I'm not doing it." As long as the CCP maintains a firm grip on the military, the armed. police, and the public security system, it still possesses a final line of defense, even if there is great chaos outside. So, you can understand why I have always maintained that the " nationalization of the military" will be one of the most important issues for China's future national transition; as long as the guns belong to a single party, the ballots in the hands of the people can never truly become the supreme power of the nation. In addition , there is another dangerous condition, which is the crisis of leadership succession. Another frequently overlooked variable is how supreme power is transferred.

Many authoritarian regimes appear very stable in normal times, but the most dangerous moments actually occur when the top leader dies suddenly, loses capacity, or enters a power transition. If the level of institutionalization is low and all power is concentrated in one person, issues will arise regarding who will succeed, who will control the military, the police, the propaganda apparatus, and the General Office, and whether different factions will settle scores with each other. Therefore, the truly most dangerous scenario for China's future is likely. not a year where GDP growth hits only 2 %, but rather the simultaneous occurrence of long-term economic recession, local fiscal crises, large-scale social protests, top-level power struggles, and succession issues— this is what is called a compounding crisis. Having said this, I must still say something that many anti-CCP friends do not like to hear: the CCP of today is not a regime that will collapse on its own tomorrow; it still possesses very strong resilience. China has massive state-owned banks, large state-owned enterprises, capital. controls, high domestic savings, world-class manufacturing, and enormous export capacity. The CCP authorities can also delay the outbreak of many problems through bond issuance, debt restructuring, financial support, fiscal transfers, and state-owned bank rollovers. Therefore, China is not exactly the same as many small emerging countries that rely on foreign dollar loans; it is not the case that if foreign capital stops lending tomorrow, China will go bankrupt the day after. This is also why the IMF's judgment on China is that the economy remains resilient, but it must address real. estate, local debt, and domestic demand structural issues, rather than declaring that China is about to collapse. So, if someone asks me today, if the Chinese economy continues like this, will the CCP fall next year? My answer would be very direct: it cannot be foreseen at the moment. On the contrary, China's most likely future may turn out to be quite boring, and the first—and perhaps most common—scenario is long-term low growth. China hasn't collapsed, nor has the CCP fallen, but the era of high-speed growth is over. Housing prices are slowly correcting, the. population is aging, youth are becoming more conservative, people are afraid to spend, and businesses are afraid to invest. Society has entered a state where people won't starve, but they no longer believe things will necessarily get better—a situation that could drag on for ten or twenty years. The second scenario is that the worse the economy gets, the tighter the politics become, with Beijing pouring more resources into national security, stability maintenance , the military, ideology, and nationalism. The result is not that poverty leads to democracy, but rather that poverty leads to more isolation. The third scenario is the truly dangerous one: a real estate crisis, a local debt crisis, a financial crisis, mass unemployment, external war or sanctions, internal power struggles within the CCP, large-scale protests, or even issues with military loyalty, all colliding at roughly the same time. If that were to happen, it wouldn't just be an ordinary economic recession; it would be a regime crisis. So, if someone tells you in the future that China's GDP is down to 3%and the CCP is about to collapse, I suggest you look at seven things: first, are local governments. defaulting on payroll long-term? Second , have bank problems spread from isolated cases to a systemic crisis? Third, has the real estate crisis spread to core financial institutions? Fourth, are protests beginning to link up across cities and provinces? Fifth, have local governments begun to openly resist the central government? Sixth, has an open and irreconcilable split emerged among the top CCP leadership? And seventh, most importantly, have the military, armed police, or public.

security forces shown signs of deviating from central orders? If China's GDP drops to 2%, but none of these latter conditions are met, I would not say the CCP is about to collapse. Conversely, if China's GDP is still at 5 %, but the fifth, sixth, and seventh conditions occur simultaneously, I would actually find it very dangerous. Because the collapse of a regime is never just an economic problem; in the end, it inevitably becomes a political one. Now we can answer the question from the beginning of the video: if China's. economy continues to slide, will the CCP really collapse? My answer is not necessarily; even if economic growth keeps slowing, it likely won't collapse immediately. But will a long-term recession weaken the CCP? The answer is yes. It will slowly erode local government finances, the confidence of the middle class, the future outlook of the youth, the investment intentions of entrepreneurs, and the legitimacy of the CCP's rule, which was built on economic performance since the Reform and Opening-up. So, an economic crisis is not the "off" switch. for the CCP's downfall; it is more like constantly pouring gasoline into a room . The gasoline piles up and the smell gets stronger, but without a spark, the house won't burn. The real sparks might be a major financial crisis, a diplomatic or military disaster, the sudden incapacitation of top leadership , infighting within the Party, large-scale mass movements, or the military and police refusing to obey orders. If this entire chain of events were to actually trigger, that would be the moment the CCP faces true danger. But in the end, there is one very. important thing I want to discuss. I have long supported the democratization of China and hope that one day the CCP’s one-party dictatorship will come to an end, but I have never believed that Chinese people must be impoverished to the point of starvation to be worthy of freedom. Sometimes, when people see the poor state of China’s economy online, they cheer, "Let housing prices fall further, let unemployment rise higher, let the economy collapse as soon as possible, so the CCP falls faster." But do not forget, if the mainland economy truly collapses, the first people to suffer will not be the. members of the Politburo Standing Committee. The first to default on mortgages will be ordinary families, the first to lose jobs will be workers and youth, the first to go bankrupt will be small businesses, and the first to worry about their retirement will be the elderly. So, if the prerequisite for the mainland’s democratization is that over a billion people must first plunge into disaster alongside the CCP, I do not believe this is a path worth looking forward to, because the Three Principles of the People has never meant destroying the mainland to start over. This is why I feel that the Three Principles of the. People, as taught by our Founding Father Sun Yat-sen, still offers a very important reminder today: because the Three Principles are not just about civil rights, they also include nationalism and the people’s livelihood . If the mainland’s economy is incredibly strong but the people can never decide who governs them, then civil rights are not realized. But if gaining civil rights first causes the country to fall into famine, civil war, and economic collapse, then the people’s livelihood is not realized either. Therefore, the democratic transition of China I envision has never been about smashing the mainland to pieces and rebuilding from the ruins. The truly. ideal path should be, while the country is still operating normally, to gradually nationalize the military, make the judiciary truly independent, allow freedom of the press, enable local self-governance, ensure fair competition among political parties, and finally, let the people use their ballots to decide who governs the central government. That is what we call a peaceful transition. So, at most, an economic crisis in the mainland can only open a door of history . It can create cracks in an otherwise.

rigid system, allow the ruling elite to start rethinking, and enable the people to begin asking whether we can truly continue on with this system. But after that door opens, will what walks through be democracy, or just another dictator? Will what walks through be constitutional government, or warlordism? Whether we walk into a free China or yet another dynastic cycle is not something that GDP figures can decide for us. Ultimately, it depends on whether the people of the mainland have organization , a civil society, new political forces. , and a system that allows different parties to compete peacefully rather than killing each other with guns. This is where I believe the National Revolution remains truly unfinished. It is not about waiting for over a billion people to go down with the regime, nor is it about hoping for another era of chaos. It is about one day returning the power that belongs to the people, without the need for famine, civil war, or the slaughter of tens of millions. An economic crisis could be fuel, or it could be the power that opens the door to history. But whether we can turn an economic crisis into a transition toward freedom ultimately depends on the people. So one day, if the CCP truly reaches a historical turning point due to prolonged economic, political, and social crises, I hope the mainland will not usher in another dynastic cycle, but rather truly complete the civil rights revolution that began over 100 years ago with the Xinhai Revolution. This road may still be very long, and the CCP will certainly not exit the stage of history just because of a year or two of poor GDP. But as long as the desire of the Chinese people for freedom , democracy, and a republic remains, the political cause of the National Revolution will not vanish due to economic prosperity, nor will it cease due to political repression. The political cause of the National Revolution may be arduous, but it will never end. Alright, that is where we will end our story for today. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析威權體制下的「政績合法性契約」，理解經濟下行如何動搖執政根基。
  • 破除「經濟變差政權便立即崩潰」的簡化迷思，從歷史脈絡與制度層面客觀審視政權轉型的關鍵門檻。
  • 揭示中國房地產與地方財政深度綁定的結構性困局，精準指出財政危機轉化為政權危機的連鎖反應。

摘要

經濟困境不等於政權崩潰：燃料與火花的本質區別

作者指出，每當官方經濟數據疲軟時，輿論常迅速興起「政權即將崩潰」的論調。然而回顧歷史，無論是過去嚴重的飢荒、文化大革命，或是北韓的極端困境，威權體制在深重災難中依然能夠延續。作者強調，經濟危機通常只是「燃料」，而非直接點燃體制崩解的「火花」。單純的經濟衰退並不足以撼動統治，唯有當危機蔓延至財政體系、引發深刻社會矛盾與體制內部撕裂，甚至波及軍警等國家暴力機器運作時，經濟問題才會真正轉化為威脅統治根基的政治危機。

經濟引擎失速：從高速狂飆轉向長期放緩

檢視當前經濟數據，作者認為中國並非瞬間撞牆倒下，而是正在經歷長期放緩的結構性轉折。過去支撐高速發展的六大支柱——人口紅利、世界工廠式的出口、外資與技術引進、房地產開發、大規模基礎建設及地方舉債模式，如今已逐漸達到邊際效應極限。當前房地產銷售滑落、內需消費疲軟與人口高齡化等現象並存，過往依靠兩位數高增長來掩蓋與消化債務的循環已難以維持，驅動經濟前進的舊引擎已面臨熄火挑戰。

地方財政危機與「威權契約」的瓦解風險

作者特別提醒，評估政權穩定度不能僅看GDP數值，核心在於「政府手中是否有充裕的資金」。在中國，房地產不僅是單一產業，更是與地方政府財政（土地財政）緊密相連的命脈。房市低迷導致土地出讓收入萎縮，但龐大的存量債務依然存在。若危機進一步導致基層公務員欠薪、公共服務停滯，甚至基層行政與維穩資源匱乏，便意味著經濟問題已開始侵蝕國家機器本身。作者總結，體制與大眾之間存在著「政績合法性」或「威權契約」——即民眾默許政治權利的讓渡，換取生活品質年年提升；一旦改善生活的承諾破滅且發展紅利耗盡，政權維繫民心的根本依據將面臨前所未有的考驗。

Let house prices fall further, let unemployment rise, the sooner the economy collapses, the sooner the CCP will fall. >> Economic deterioration does increase pressure, but can it truly lead to a regime transition? In political science, this exchange under an authoritarian system is called a "performance-based legitimacy" contract. People accept limited political participation, while the regime trades economic performance, security, and benefits for stability. But this exchange has a major prerequisite. Life must truly keep getting better. If it starts to become a reality where house prices keep dropping, wages stagnate, college graduates can't find ideal jobs, business becomes harder, and the next generation feels they can't possibly be wealthier than their parents , then people will start asking: You told me we couldn't do without the Communist Party because it could develop China. But if development slows down today, what does the CCP have left to maintain the hearts and minds of the people? People often ask about the map in my background. This map isn't just my dream. for the territory of the Republic of China; it’s what the Republic of China should look like in the eyes of all 1.4 billion Chinese descendants. We aim to restore the Republic of China, using the Three Principles of the People from the National Revolution to fulfill the mission of reclaiming the Republic and rebuilding the nation. We have launched a product bundle featuring map posters, tapestries, throw pillows, and ROC flag keychains. Why choose? Get them all for just 1911. Also, on both platforms, orders over 699 get free shipping. Friends overseas don't worry, we will launch international purchasing options soon, so hurry up and grab yours! >> Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. Over the past few years, whenever the CCP official. releases lackluster economic figures, the internet immediately erupts with " The CCP is about to collapse!" Real estate falls, the CCP is about to collapse! Youth can't find jobs, the CCP is about to collapse! Local governments in debt, the CCP is about to collapse! Consumption is weak, the CCP is about to collapse. Sometimes, even if the A-shares drop for a few days, people start calculating, "At this speed, does the CCP only have three years left?" The question is, will an authoritarian regime really collapse just because the economy is bad? If it were that simple, the CCP would have collapsed countless times already. In the past, the mainland experienced economic and food disasters far worse than today, yet the CCP didn't collapse . The Cultural Revolution turned Chinese society upside down, yet the CCP didn't collapse. North Korea went through severe famine, yet the Kim regime didn't collapse. There are many authoritarian governments worldwide that have survived for years despite severe economic crises. So today, the real question we should be. asking isn't whether China's economy will keep getting worse, but rather how bad it has to get before it turns into a political crisis that truly shakes the CCP's grip on power? These two things are completely different. I’ll give you the most important answer upfront: an economic crisis is fuel, but it’s usually not the spark that topples an authoritarian regime. The real danger arises when an economic crisis spirals into a fiscal crisis, a social crisis, and infighting within the Party, eventually causing issues even within the military and. police—the coercive apparatus that maintains the regime. Only when it reaches that point can an economic collapse potentially lead to political collapse. Before we rush to wait for the CCP to fall, let's look at how bad the Chinese economy actually is right now. In the first half of 2026, the official GDP growth announced by the CCP was 4.7%—5% in the first quarter, dropping to 4.3% in the second. For many mature economies, 4.7%is actually quite high, so if someone tells you that the Chinese economy has.

completely collapsed and will turn into the Soviet Union tomorrow, they are clearly jumping the gun. But if someone else tells you that because GDP is still at 4.7%, there are no problems at all with the Chinese economy, that is equally naive. Because the real problem for China today is not whether there is growth, but whether the engines that drove that high-speed growth in the past can still keep running. Let’s look at a few numbers: in the first seven months of 2026, total retail. sales of consumer goods in China grew by only 1.2%, with a mere 0.6%increase in July alone. The issues in real estate are even more apparent; in the first seven months of this year, sales of newly built commercial housing fell by 13.1%year-on-year, and funding for real estate developers dropped by 20.3%. On the other hand, Chinese exports still show considerable resilience, with official figures showing 14%growth in the first seven months of this year, while the national urban unemployment rate remains at around 5.2%. So, if I had to describe China today in one sentence: it hasn't hit a wall suddenly, but is experiencing a long-term slowdown. China used to be a car used to racing at 150 km/h; now it has slowed down to 80 or 90. The car is still moving and the engine hasn't stalled, but the trouble is that there might be a very long downhill slope ahead. What has China’s high-speed economic growth relied on since the Reform and Opening-up? Simply put, it’s a few things: First, the demographic dividend, with waves of. young people entering factories. Second , exports, as China became the world’s factory. Third, foreign capital and technology, with companies shifting supply chains to China. Fourth, real estate, where local governments sell land, developers build houses, banks issue loans, and families buy them. Fifth, infrastructure, with highways, high-speed rail, airports, and industrial parks being built rapidly. Sixth, local government debt, where they borrow to build, hoping future growth will digest the debt. The biggest feature of this entire model. is that as long as the economy keeps growing at a high speed, many problems can be masked by that growth. 110 billion might seem scary today, but if GDP grows by 10%next year and land prices rise, it doesn't seem like such a big problem anymore. But now the trouble has arrived: the population is aging, the real estate sector is declining, local governments are heavily in debt, household consumption is insufficient, and the marginal utility of investment is getting worse. In its 2024 assessment of China, the IMF also specifically pointed out that the ongoing real estate. adjustment, high debt, weak domestic demand, and factors related to population and productivity will all drag down China's medium-to-long-term growth potential. So the real question to ask now is no longer whether it’s 4.5%or 5%this year, but rather, if this formula that powered China for the last 40 years has truly reached its end, what will the CCP rely on to maintain its rule for the next 20 years? I think the point most people easily overlook is that when we look at China's. economy, we often just look at GDP. But if you want to judge whether a regime is in danger, I would look at whether the government itself has money , because for China, real estate isn't just a regular industry; it is tied to local government finances. In the past, a major source of revenue for many local governments was selling land: developers bought land, borrowed from banks, built houses, and citizens bought them. Local governments collected land revenue and used it to build new roads, industrial parks, and subways. So when real estate was booming, everyone.

felt rich: local governments had money, developers had money, banks felt secure , and homeowners felt their properties were becoming more valuable year by year . But what about now? Houses are hard to sell, developers don't dare to acquire land, and local land revenue is falling . However, the debt borrowed previously won't disappear just because housing prices dropped, so local governments are now facing a very troublesome question: where will the money come from? This is why the IMF keeps emphasizing that China's local government and local. financing platform debts need further handling. When will this issue turn from economic news into political news? If a locality builds one less stadium, the CCP won't collapse; if they hold one less fireworks show, it won't either. But if one day a large number of regions start delaying civil servant salaries, slashing teacher compensation, facing problems with healthcare and social security, defaulting on payments to private enterprises, seeing public service quality decline, or even having basic administrative and police. operations affected by finances, then the nature of the situation changes. Because this means the economic crisis has begun to erode the state apparatus itself; that is why I have always believed that for the people it is a livelihood issue, but when the government runs out of money, it starts to become a regime issue. Since the reform and opening-up, the CCP has essentially formed an unwritten political bargain with many mainlanders , which can be summarized as: "You don't challenge my rule, and I will make your life better year by year." You cannot vote to replace the Communist Party, but your income increases, you can buy homes, cars, travel abroad, your children can go to college, and China's national strength grows day by day. So even if many people are dissatisfied with politics, they figure it's fine, as long as life is still improving. In political science, this type of exchange under an authoritarian system is called an "authoritarian contract," where the public accepts limited political participation, and the regime trades economic performance, security, and benefit distribution for legitimacy. . But there is one major prerequisite to this exchange: life must genuinely keep getting better. If property values start to plummet, wages stagnate, college graduates cannot find ideal jobs, doing business becomes increasingly difficult, and the next generation feels they will never be as wealthy as their parents, then people will begin to ask: "You told me we couldn't do without the Party because it ensures development, so if development slows down today, what does the CCP have left to maintain stability?" This doesn't mean the people will revolt , but it will slowly erode a crucial pillar of the CCP's legitimacy since the reform and opening-up. Let's first discuss: if people become poorer, will they really revolt? The answer is not necessarily; in fact, most of the time they won't. In democratic countries, if the economy is poor, the people have a clear exit: they can change the government. If a president fails, they step down in four years; if the ruling party ruins the economy, they switch to another party in the next election. But in a one-party. dictatorship, there is no such exit. So , what do the people do? Some choose to "lie flat," some decide not to have children, and some cut back on consumption. Others take civil service exams, try to emigrate, or complain online all day. But complaining and revolution are two entirely different things. Suppose there are 10 million people in the mainland today cursing the Communist Party at home, but they don't know each other, have no organization, no leaders , no funds, no media, and no cross-city connection. The political threat of those 10 million.

might be less than that of 100,000 people who are truly organized. Therefore, what an authoritarian regime fears most is not that the people are dissatisfied, but that they begin to organize. This is why the CCP is particularly sensitive toward independent labor unions, cross-regional social movements, independent media, and political organizations. Because when one person curses the government at home , it is just an emotion; but when a group of people begins to make demands together, that is politics. So, never assume that if China's economy is bad, the people will demand reform and the. CCP will be forced to democratize. History does not guarantee this path at all. There is another possibility: because the economy is poor, people are dissatisfied, and the regime feels society is unstable, it may then strengthen stability maintenance, tighten speech control, emphasize national security even more, and stress nationalism. Ultimately, instead of becoming democratic, it becomes more centralized. Furthermore, economic problems can be reinterpreted—why is China's economy poor? It is not that our policies have problems; it is that the United States is suppressing China, the. West is containing China, and foreign powers do not want the Chinese nation to rise. Therefore, we must not be in chaos now, and the people nationwide must unite even more closely around the Party Central Committee. This narrative is crucial for an authoritarian system because it can transform dissatisfaction with the government into anger toward external enemies. So, a very counter-intuitive conclusion is that economic decline sometimes does not lead to political opening, but may instead lead to even tougher political control. If we look back at the CCP's own history , it becomes very clear: during the. Great Leap Forward, the lives of mainland people were much more difficult than today. That was a truly massive humanitarian disaster, but the CCP did not fall. Why ? Because the Party remained, the military remained, the public security forces remained, and the local administrative systems remained. The people also lacked any independent organization that could span the entire country to replace the Communist Party. The Cultural Revolution was the same: the entire society suffered massive destruction, and China even fell into severe political chaos, but in the end,. the Communist Party still reclaimed order. Therefore, we must face a very cruel fact: if just economic downturns and the suffering of the masses were enough to topple the CCP, then the CCP would have already fallen in the 1960s. This is why political science research usually does not regard economic crisis as a single sufficient condition for the collapse of an authoritarian regime. Economic deterioration increases pressure, but whether it can truly cause a regime transition also depends on ruling elites, social organizations, and. the regime's control capabilities, among other things. When will an economic crisis truly turn into a political crisis? I believe we must look at at least a few conditions. The first is when cross-class dissatisfaction begins to converge. Normally, a young person who cannot find work only thinks it is a youth problem; a homeowner whose property value drops thinks it is a real estate problem; an entrepreneur who cannot make money thinks it is a business environment problem; a local civil servant who is unpaid thinks it is a local fiscal problem; and retirees worried about health insurance think it is a social security problem. But what is truly. dangerous is when these people suddenly start to feel that our problems are actually the same problem, and in the end, they all point to the same system. At this point, economic dissatisfaction will truly begin to be politicized. The second truly dangerous condition is when the Communist Party itself splits. I think this is even more important than how many people are protesting on the streets. An authoritarian regime is at its strongest not when no one dislikes it, but when the ruling elite is highly united, and everyone believes that staying with the regime is still in.

their best interest. However, the most troublesome aspect of an economic crisis is that the pie gets smaller. In the past, when the economy grew by 8%annually, the central government could get a share, local governments could get a share, state-owned enterprises could get a share; officials had political achievements, and entrepreneurs made money. Even if everyone was annoyed with each other, there was at least more and more food on the table. What if the economy stagnates today? Then the problem arises: who is going to swallow the losses? Local governments, the central government, state banks, private enterprises, the middle class, homeowners—who is ultimately going to. foot the bill for local debts? Research in political science on authoritarian systems also points out that elite unity is, in itself, an essential pillar of regime stability. And when economic performance worsens and the distribution of benefits becomes uncertain, some members of the ruling elite are more likely to consider abandoning the original regime coalition. Therefore, what could truly endanger the CCP is not just the public realizing they are broke , but the day when even people inside the Communist Party start to feel that " if we keep following this system, I will lose my money, my power, and perhaps. even my life." At this point, everyone starts looking for an exit. Some advocate for reform, some for changing leaders, some try to push the blame onto others, and some start secretly contacting external forces. Once it reaches this stage, an economic crisis truly becomes a crisis of power. The third condition is that opposition forces begin to organize. But intra-party strife alone is not enough; society must develop real organizational capabilities. For example, students, workers, the. middle class, local rights activists, intellectuals, and entrepreneurs— different groups must stop complaining in isolation and start forming common political demands. What is even more important is cross-city coordination. A protest of 1,000 people in Shanghai might not shake the central government, but if after something happens in Shanghai, Beijing responds, Guangzhou responds, Chengdu responds, and Wuhan responds, and they start to have common slogans, common leadership, and common political demands, the nature of the situation changes entirely because it is. no longer a mass incident, but a nationwide political movement. The fourth condition is whether those who hold the guns are still obedient. The final hurdle is usually the most realistic and cruel one: the military and the public security apparatus. 1989 is actually a very important example. At that time, there was inflation and corruption, demands for political reform , and large-scale student and citizen movements. Even the highest levels of the CCP had serious divisions on how to handle the movement. So you see, mass mobilization was there , social discontent was there, political demands were there, and a split at the top also occurred, but in the end, the CCP did not fall. Why? One critical reason is that the military ultimately continues to carry out the hardline policies of the center ; thus, for many authoritarian regimes, the true moment of collapse is not when people first take to the streets, but when the military and police first tell their top leader, "This time, I'm not doing it." As long as the CCP maintains a firm grip on the military, the armed. police, and the public security system, it still possesses a final line of defense, even if there is great chaos outside. So, you can understand why I have always maintained that the " nationalization of the military" will be one of the most important issues for China's future national transition; as long as the guns belong to a single party, the ballots in the hands of the people can never truly become the supreme power of the nation. In addition , there is another dangerous condition, which is the crisis of leadership succession. Another frequently overlooked variable is how supreme power is transferred.

Many authoritarian regimes appear very stable in normal times, but the most dangerous moments actually occur when the top leader dies suddenly, loses capacity, or enters a power transition. If the level of institutionalization is low and all power is concentrated in one person, issues will arise regarding who will succeed, who will control the military, the police, the propaganda apparatus, and the General Office, and whether different factions will settle scores with each other. Therefore, the truly most dangerous scenario for China's future is likely. not a year where GDP growth hits only 2 %, but rather the simultaneous occurrence of long-term economic recession, local fiscal crises, large-scale social protests, top-level power struggles, and succession issues— this is what is called a compounding crisis. Having said this, I must still say something that many anti-CCP friends do not like to hear: the CCP of today is not a regime that will collapse on its own tomorrow; it still possesses very strong resilience. China has massive state-owned banks, large state-owned enterprises, capital. controls, high domestic savings, world-class manufacturing, and enormous export capacity. The CCP authorities can also delay the outbreak of many problems through bond issuance, debt restructuring, financial support, fiscal transfers, and state-owned bank rollovers. Therefore, China is not exactly the same as many small emerging countries that rely on foreign dollar loans; it is not the case that if foreign capital stops lending tomorrow, China will go bankrupt the day after. This is also why the IMF's judgment on China is that the economy remains resilient, but it must address real. estate, local debt, and domestic demand structural issues, rather than declaring that China is about to collapse. So, if someone asks me today, if the Chinese economy continues like this, will the CCP fall next year? My answer would be very direct: it cannot be foreseen at the moment. On the contrary, China's most likely future may turn out to be quite boring, and the first—and perhaps most common—scenario is long-term low growth. China hasn't collapsed, nor has the CCP fallen, but the era of high-speed growth is over. Housing prices are slowly correcting, the. population is aging, youth are becoming more conservative, people are afraid to spend, and businesses are afraid to invest. Society has entered a state where people won't starve, but they no longer believe things will necessarily get better—a situation that could drag on for ten or twenty years. The second scenario is that the worse the economy gets, the tighter the politics become, with Beijing pouring more resources into national security, stability maintenance , the military, ideology, and nationalism. The result is not that poverty leads to democracy, but rather that poverty leads to more isolation. The third scenario is the truly dangerous one: a real estate crisis, a local debt crisis, a financial crisis, mass unemployment, external war or sanctions, internal power struggles within the CCP, large-scale protests, or even issues with military loyalty, all colliding at roughly the same time. If that were to happen, it wouldn't just be an ordinary economic recession; it would be a regime crisis. So, if someone tells you in the future that China's GDP is down to 3%and the CCP is about to collapse, I suggest you look at seven things: first, are local governments. defaulting on payroll long-term? Second , have bank problems spread from isolated cases to a systemic crisis? Third, has the real estate crisis spread to core financial institutions? Fourth, are protests beginning to link up across cities and provinces? Fifth, have local governments begun to openly resist the central government? Sixth, has an open and irreconcilable split emerged among the top CCP leadership? And seventh, most importantly, have the military, armed police, or public.

security forces shown signs of deviating from central orders? If China's GDP drops to 2%, but none of these latter conditions are met, I would not say the CCP is about to collapse. Conversely, if China's GDP is still at 5 %, but the fifth, sixth, and seventh conditions occur simultaneously, I would actually find it very dangerous. Because the collapse of a regime is never just an economic problem; in the end, it inevitably becomes a political one. Now we can answer the question from the beginning of the video: if China's. economy continues to slide, will the CCP really collapse? My answer is not necessarily; even if economic growth keeps slowing, it likely won't collapse immediately. But will a long-term recession weaken the CCP? The answer is yes. It will slowly erode local government finances, the confidence of the middle class, the future outlook of the youth, the investment intentions of entrepreneurs, and the legitimacy of the CCP's rule, which was built on economic performance since the Reform and Opening-up. So, an economic crisis is not the "off" switch. for the CCP's downfall; it is more like constantly pouring gasoline into a room . The gasoline piles up and the smell gets stronger, but without a spark, the house won't burn. The real sparks might be a major financial crisis, a diplomatic or military disaster, the sudden incapacitation of top leadership , infighting within the Party, large-scale mass movements, or the military and police refusing to obey orders. If this entire chain of events were to actually trigger, that would be the moment the CCP faces true danger. But in the end, there is one very. important thing I want to discuss. I have long supported the democratization of China and hope that one day the CCP’s one-party dictatorship will come to an end, but I have never believed that Chinese people must be impoverished to the point of starvation to be worthy of freedom. Sometimes, when people see the poor state of China’s economy online, they cheer, "Let housing prices fall further, let unemployment rise higher, let the economy collapse as soon as possible, so the CCP falls faster." But do not forget, if the mainland economy truly collapses, the first people to suffer will not be the. members of the Politburo Standing Committee. The first to default on mortgages will be ordinary families, the first to lose jobs will be workers and youth, the first to go bankrupt will be small businesses, and the first to worry about their retirement will be the elderly. So, if the prerequisite for the mainland’s democratization is that over a billion people must first plunge into disaster alongside the CCP, I do not believe this is a path worth looking forward to, because the Three Principles of the People has never meant destroying the mainland to start over. This is why I feel that the Three Principles of the. People, as taught by our Founding Father Sun Yat-sen, still offers a very important reminder today: because the Three Principles are not just about civil rights, they also include nationalism and the people’s livelihood . If the mainland’s economy is incredibly strong but the people can never decide who governs them, then civil rights are not realized. But if gaining civil rights first causes the country to fall into famine, civil war, and economic collapse, then the people’s livelihood is not realized either. Therefore, the democratic transition of China I envision has never been about smashing the mainland to pieces and rebuilding from the ruins. The truly. ideal path should be, while the country is still operating normally, to gradually nationalize the military, make the judiciary truly independent, allow freedom of the press, enable local self-governance, ensure fair competition among political parties, and finally, let the people use their ballots to decide who governs the central government. That is what we call a peaceful transition. So, at most, an economic crisis in the mainland can only open a door of history . It can create cracks in an otherwise.

rigid system, allow the ruling elite to start rethinking, and enable the people to begin asking whether we can truly continue on with this system. But after that door opens, will what walks through be democracy, or just another dictator? Will what walks through be constitutional government, or warlordism? Whether we walk into a free China or yet another dynastic cycle is not something that GDP figures can decide for us. Ultimately, it depends on whether the people of the mainland have organization , a civil society, new political forces. , and a system that allows different parties to compete peacefully rather than killing each other with guns. This is where I believe the National Revolution remains truly unfinished. It is not about waiting for over a billion people to go down with the regime, nor is it about hoping for another era of chaos. It is about one day returning the power that belongs to the people, without the need for famine, civil war, or the slaughter of tens of millions. An economic crisis could be fuel, or it could be the power that opens the door to history. But whether we can turn an economic crisis into a transition toward freedom ultimately depends on the people. So one day, if the CCP truly reaches a historical turning point due to prolonged economic, political, and social crises, I hope the mainland will not usher in another dynastic cycle, but rather truly complete the civil rights revolution that began over 100 years ago with the Xinhai Revolution. This road may still be very long, and the CCP will certainly not exit the stage of history just because of a year or two of poor GDP. But as long as the desire of the Chinese people for freedom , democracy, and a republic remains, the political cause of the National Revolution will not vanish due to economic prosperity, nor will it cease due to political repression. The political cause of the National Revolution may be arduous, but it will never end. Alright, that is where we will end our story for today. If you enjoyed this episode, please help us by clicking subscribe and sharing it. We are also incredibly grateful to those who are able to join as members. Additionally, our Discord and Telegram. groups are now open, where you can receive our updates in real-time, and we welcome everyone to join in the conversation. That is all for today’s study notes. We will see you next time, bye-bye.

值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入剖析威權體制下的「政績合法性契約」，理解經濟下行如何動搖執政根基。
  • 破除「經濟變差政權便立即崩潰」的簡化迷思，從歷史脈絡與制度層面客觀審視政權轉型的關鍵門檻。
  • 揭示中國房地產與地方財政深度綁定的結構性困局，精準指出財政危機轉化為政權危機的連鎖反應。

摘要

經濟困境不等於政權崩潰：燃料與火花的本質區別

作者指出，每當官方經濟數據疲軟時，輿論常迅速興起「政權即將崩潰」的論調。然而回顧歷史，無論是過去嚴重的飢荒、文化大革命，或是北韓的極端困境，威權體制在深重災難中依然能夠延續。作者強調，經濟危機通常只是「燃料」，而非直接點燃體制崩解的「火花」。單純的經濟衰退並不足以撼動統治，唯有當危機蔓延至財政體系、引發深刻社會矛盾與體制內部撕裂，甚至波及軍警等國家暴力機器運作時，經濟問題才會真正轉化為威脅統治根基的政治危機。

經濟引擎失速：從高速狂飆轉向長期放緩

檢視當前經濟數據，作者認為中國並非瞬間撞牆倒下，而是正在經歷長期放緩的結構性轉折。過去支撐高速發展的六大支柱——人口紅利、世界工廠式的出口、外資與技術引進、房地產開發、大規模基礎建設及地方舉債模式，如今已逐漸達到邊際效應極限。當前房地產銷售滑落、內需消費疲軟與人口高齡化等現象並存，過往依靠兩位數高增長來掩蓋與消化債務的循環已難以維持，驅動經濟前進的舊引擎已面臨熄火挑戰。

地方財政危機與「威權契約」的瓦解風險

作者特別提醒，評估政權穩定度不能僅看GDP數值，核心在於「政府手中是否有充裕的資金」。在中國，房地產不僅是單一產業，更是與地方政府財政（土地財政）緊密相連的命脈。房市低迷導致土地出讓收入萎縮，但龐大的存量債務依然存在。若危機進一步導致基層公務員欠薪、公共服務停滯，甚至基層行政與維穩資源匱乏，便意味著經濟問題已開始侵蝕國家機器本身。作者總結，體制與大眾之間存在著「政績合法性」或「威權契約」——即民眾默許政治權利的讓渡，換取生活品質年年提升；一旦改善生活的承諾破滅且發展紅利耗盡，政權維繫民心的根本依據將面臨前所未有的考驗。

================================================

Let house prices fall further, let unemployment rise, the sooner the economy collapses, the sooner the CCP will fall. >> Economic deterioration does increase pressure, but can it truly lead to a regime transition? In political science, this exchange under an authoritarian system is called a "performance-based legitimacy" contract. People accept limited political participation, while the regime trades economic performance, security, and benefits for stability. But this exchange has a major prerequisite. Life must truly keep getting better. If it starts to become a reality where house prices keep dropping, wages stagnate, college graduates can't find ideal jobs, business becomes harder, and the next generation feels they can't possibly be wealthier than their parents , then people will start asking: You told me we couldn't do without the Communist Party because it could develop China. But if development slows down today, what does the CCP have left to maintain the hearts and minds of the people? People often ask about the map in my background. This map isn't just my dream. for the territory of the Republic of China; it’s what the Republic of China should look like in the eyes of all 1.4 billion Chinese descendants.
