Also, on both platforms, orders over 699 get free shipping. Friends overseas don't worry, we will launch international purchasing options soon, so hurry up and grab yours! >> Hello everyone, I’m A-Niu. Over the past few years, whenever the CCP official. releases lackluster economic figures, the internet immediately erupts with " The CCP is about to collapse!" Real estate falls, the CCP is about to collapse! Youth can't find jobs, the CCP is about to collapse! Local governments in debt, the CCP is about to collapse! Consumption is weak, the CCP is about to collapse. Sometimes, even if the A-shares drop for a few days, people start calculating, "At this speed, does the CCP only have three years left?" The question is, will an authoritarian regime really collapse just because the economy is bad? If it were that simple, the CCP would have collapsed countless times already. In the past, the mainland experienced economic and food disasters far worse than today, yet the CCP didn't collapse . The Cultural Revolution turned Chinese society upside down, yet the CCP didn't collapse. North Korea went through severe famine, yet the Kim regime didn't collapse. There are many authoritarian governments worldwide that have survived for years despite severe economic crises. So today, the real question we should be. asking isn't whether China's economy will keep getting worse, but rather how bad it has to get before it turns into a political crisis that truly shakes the CCP's grip on power? These two things are completely different. I’ll give you the most important answer upfront: an economic crisis is fuel, but it’s usually not the spark that topples an authoritarian regime. The real danger arises when an economic crisis spirals into a fiscal crisis, a social crisis, and infighting within the Party, eventually causing issues even within the military and. police—the coercive apparatus that maintains the regime. Only when it reaches that point can an economic collapse potentially lead to political collapse. Before we rush to wait for the CCP to fall, let's look at how bad the Chinese economy actually is right now. In the first half of 2026, the official GDP growth announced by the CCP was 4.7%—5% in the first quarter, dropping to 4.3% in the second. For many mature economies, 4.7%is actually quite high, so if someone tells you that the Chinese economy has.

completely collapsed and will turn into the Soviet Union tomorrow, they are clearly jumping the gun. But if someone else tells you that because GDP is still at 4.7%, there are no problems at all with the Chinese economy, that is equally naive. Because the real problem for China today is not whether there is growth, but whether the engines that drove that high-speed growth in the past can still keep running. Let’s look at a few numbers: in the first seven months of 2026, total retail. sales of consumer goods in China grew by only 1.2%, with a mere 0.6%increase in July alone. The issues in real estate are even more apparent; in the first seven months of this year, sales of newly built commercial housing fell by 13.1%year-on-year, and funding for real estate developers dropped by 20.3%. On the other hand, Chinese exports still show considerable resilience, with official figures showing 14%growth in the first seven months of this year, while the national urban unemployment rate remains at around 5.2%. So, if I had to describe China today in one sentence: it hasn't hit a wall suddenly, but is experiencing a long-term slowdown. China used to be a car used to racing at 150 km/h; now it has slowed down to 80 or 90. The car is still moving and the engine hasn't stalled, but the trouble is that there might be a very long downhill slope ahead. What has China’s high-speed economic growth relied on since the Reform and Opening-up? Simply put, it’s a few things: First, the demographic dividend, with waves of. young people entering factories. Second , exports, as China became the world’s factory. Third, foreign capital and technology, with companies shifting supply chains to China. Fourth, real estate, where local governments sell land, developers build houses, banks issue loans, and families buy them. Fifth, infrastructure, with highways, high-speed rail, airports, and industrial parks being built rapidly. Sixth, local government debt, where they borrow to build, hoping future growth will digest the debt. The biggest feature of this entire model. is that as long as the economy keeps growing at a high speed, many problems can be masked by that growth. 110 billion might seem scary today, but if GDP grows by 10%next year and land prices rise, it doesn't seem like such a big problem anymore. But now the trouble has arrived: the population is aging, the real estate sector is declining, local governments are heavily in debt, household consumption is insufficient, and the marginal utility of investment is getting worse. In its 2024 assessment of China, the IMF also specifically pointed out that the ongoing real estate. adjustment, high debt, weak domestic demand, and factors related to population and productivity will all drag down China's medium-to-long-term growth potential. So the real question to ask now is no longer whether it’s 4.5%or 5%this year, but rather, if this formula that powered China for the last 40 years has truly reached its end, what will the CCP rely on to maintain its rule for the next 20 years? I think the point most people easily overlook is that when we look at China's. economy, we often just look at GDP. But if you want to judge whether a regime is in danger, I would look at whether the government itself has money , because for China, real estate isn't just a regular industry; it is tied to local government finances. In the past, a major source of revenue for many local governments was selling land: developers bought land, borrowed from banks, built houses, and citizens bought them. Local governments collected land revenue and used it to build new roads, industrial parks, and subways. So when real estate was booming, everyone.

felt rich: local governments had money, developers had money, banks felt secure , and homeowners felt their properties were becoming more valuable year by year . But what about now? Houses are hard to sell, developers don't dare to acquire land, and local land revenue is falling . However, the debt borrowed previously won't disappear just because housing prices dropped, so local governments are now facing a very troublesome question: where will the money come from? This is why the IMF keeps emphasizing that China's local government and local. financing platform debts need further handling. When will this issue turn from economic news into political news? If a locality builds one less stadium, the CCP won't collapse; if they hold one less fireworks show, it won't either. But if one day a large number of regions start delaying civil servant salaries, slashing teacher compensation, facing problems with healthcare and social security, defaulting on payments to private enterprises, seeing public service quality decline, or even having basic administrative and police. operations affected by finances, then the nature of the situation changes. Because this means the economic crisis has begun to erode the state apparatus itself; that is why I have always believed that for the people it is a livelihood issue, but when the government runs out of money, it starts to become a regime issue. Since the reform and opening-up, the CCP has essentially formed an unwritten political bargain with many mainlanders , which can be summarized as: "You don't challenge my rule, and I will make your life better year by year." You cannot vote to replace the Communist Party, but your income increases, you can buy homes, cars, travel abroad, your children can go to college, and China's national strength grows day by day. So even if many people are dissatisfied with politics, they figure it's fine, as long as life is still improving. In political science, this type of exchange under an authoritarian system is called an "authoritarian contract," where the public accepts limited political participation, and the regime trades economic performance, security, and benefit distribution for legitimacy. . But there is one major prerequisite to this exchange: life must genuinely keep getting better. If property values start to plummet, wages stagnate, college graduates cannot find ideal jobs, doing business becomes increasingly difficult, and the next generation feels they will never be as wealthy as their parents, then people will begin to ask: "You told me we couldn't do without the Party because it ensures development, so if development slows down today, what does the CCP have left to maintain stability?" This doesn't mean the people will revolt , but it will slowly erode a crucial pillar of the CCP's legitimacy since the reform and opening-up. Let's first discuss: if people become poorer, will they really revolt? The answer is not necessarily; in fact, most of the time they won't. In democratic countries, if the economy is poor, the people have a clear exit: they can change the government. If a president fails, they step down in four years; if the ruling party ruins the economy, they switch to another party in the next election. But in a one-party. dictatorship, there is no such exit. So , what do the people do? Some choose to "lie flat," some decide not to have children, and some cut back on consumption. Others take civil service exams, try to emigrate, or complain online all day. But complaining and revolution are two entirely different things. Suppose there are 10 million people in the mainland today cursing the Communist Party at home, but they don't know each other, have no organization, no leaders , no funds, no media, and no cross-city connection. The political threat of those 10 million.

might be less than that of 100,000 people who are truly organized. Therefore, what an authoritarian regime fears most is not that the people are dissatisfied, but that they begin to organize. This is why the CCP is particularly sensitive toward independent labor unions, cross-regional social movements, independent media, and political organizations. Because when one person curses the government at home , it is just an emotion; but when a group of people begins to make demands together, that is politics. So, never assume that if China's economy is bad, the people will demand reform and the. CCP will be forced to democratize. History does not guarantee this path at all. There is another possibility: because the economy is poor, people are dissatisfied, and the regime feels society is unstable, it may then strengthen stability maintenance, tighten speech control, emphasize national security even more, and stress nationalism. Ultimately, instead of becoming democratic, it becomes more centralized. Furthermore, economic problems can be reinterpreted—why is China's economy poor? It is not that our policies have problems; it is that the United States is suppressing China, the. West is containing China, and foreign powers do not want the Chinese nation to rise. Therefore, we must not be in chaos now, and the people nationwide must unite even more closely around the Party Central Committee. This narrative is crucial for an authoritarian system because it can transform dissatisfaction with the government into anger toward external enemies. So, a very counter-intuitive conclusion is that economic decline sometimes does not lead to political opening, but may instead lead to even tougher political control. If we look back at the CCP's own history , it becomes very clear: during the. Great Leap Forward, the lives of mainland people were much more difficult than today. That was a truly massive humanitarian disaster, but the CCP did not fall. Why ? Because the Party remained, the military remained, the public security forces remained, and the local administrative systems remained. The people also lacked any independent organization that could span the entire country to replace the Communist Party. The Cultural Revolution was the same: the entire society suffered massive destruction, and China even fell into severe political chaos, but in the end,. the Communist Party still reclaimed order. Therefore, we must face a very cruel fact: if just economic downturns and the suffering of the masses were enough to topple the CCP, then the CCP would have already fallen in the 1960s. This is why political science research usually does not regard economic crisis as a single sufficient condition for the collapse of an authoritarian regime. Economic deterioration increases pressure, but whether it can truly cause a regime transition also depends on ruling elites, social organizations, and. the regime's control capabilities, among other things. When will an economic crisis truly turn into a political crisis? I believe we must look at at least a few conditions. The first is when cross-class dissatisfaction begins to converge. Normally, a young person who cannot find work only thinks it is a youth problem; a homeowner whose property value drops thinks it is a real estate problem; an entrepreneur who cannot make money thinks it is a business environment problem; a local civil servant who is unpaid thinks it is a local fiscal problem; and retirees worried about health insurance think it is a social security problem. But what is truly. dangerous is when these people suddenly start to feel that our problems are actually the same problem, and in the end, they all point to the same system. At this point, economic dissatisfaction will truly begin to be politicized. The second truly dangerous condition is when the Communist Party itself splits. I think this is even more important than how many people are protesting on the streets. An authoritarian regime is at its strongest not when no one dislikes it, but when the ruling elite is highly united, and everyone believes that staying with the regime is still in.

their best interest. However, the most troublesome aspect of an economic crisis is that the pie gets smaller. In the past, when the economy grew by 8%annually, the central government could get a share, local governments could get a share, state-owned enterprises could get a share; officials had political achievements, and entrepreneurs made money. Even if everyone was annoyed with each other, there was at least more and more food on the table. What if the economy stagnates today? Then the problem arises: who is going to swallow the losses? Local governments, the central government, state banks, private enterprises, the middle class, homeowners—who is ultimately going to. foot the bill for local debts? Research in political science on authoritarian systems also points out that elite unity is, in itself, an essential pillar of regime stability. And when economic performance worsens and the distribution of benefits becomes uncertain, some members of the ruling elite are more likely to consider abandoning the original regime coalition. Therefore, what could truly endanger the CCP is not just the public realizing they are broke , but the day when even people inside the Communist Party start to feel that " if we keep following this system, I will lose my money, my power, and perhaps. even my life." At this point, everyone starts looking for an exit. Some advocate for reform, some for changing leaders, some try to push the blame onto others, and some start secretly contacting external forces. Once it reaches this stage, an economic crisis truly becomes a crisis of power. The third condition is that opposition forces begin to organize. But intra-party strife alone is not enough; society must develop real organizational capabilities. For example, students, workers, the. middle class, local rights activists, intellectuals, and entrepreneurs— different groups must stop complaining in isolation and start forming common political demands. What is even more important is cross-city coordination. A protest of 1,000 people in Shanghai might not shake the central government, but if after something happens in Shanghai, Beijing responds, Guangzhou responds, Chengdu responds, and Wuhan responds, and they start to have common slogans, common leadership, and common political demands, the nature of the situation changes entirely because it is. no longer a mass incident, but a nationwide political movement. The fourth condition is whether those who hold the guns are still obedient. The final hurdle is usually the most realistic and cruel one: the military and the public security apparatus. 1989 is actually a very important example. At that time, there was inflation and corruption, demands for political reform , and large-scale student and citizen movements. Even the highest levels of the CCP had serious divisions on how to handle the movement. So you see, mass mobilization was there , social discontent was there, political demands were there, and a split at the top also occurred, but in the end, the CCP did not fall. Why? One critical reason is that the military ultimately continues to carry out the hardline policies of the center ; thus, for many authoritarian regimes, the true moment of collapse is not when people first take to the streets, but when the military and police first tell their top leader, "This time, I'm not doing it." As long as the CCP maintains a firm grip on the military, the armed. police, and the public security system, it still possesses a final line of defense, even if there is great chaos outside. So, you can understand why I have always maintained that the " nationalization of the military" will be one of the most important issues for China's future national transition; as long as the guns belong to a single party, the ballots in the hands of the people can never truly become the supreme power of the nation. In addition , there is another dangerous condition, which is the crisis of leadership succession. Another frequently overlooked variable is how supreme power is transferred.

Many authoritarian regimes appear very stable in normal times, but the most dangerous moments actually occur when the top leader dies suddenly, loses capacity, or enters a power transition. If the level of institutionalization is low and all power is concentrated in one person, issues will arise regarding who will succeed, who will control the military, the police, the propaganda apparatus, and the General Office, and whether different factions will settle scores with each other. Therefore, the truly most dangerous scenario for China's future is likely. not a year where GDP growth hits only 2 %, but rather the simultaneous occurrence of long-term economic recession, local fiscal crises, large-scale social protests, top-level power struggles, and succession issues— this is what is called a compounding crisis. Having said this, I must still say something that many anti-CCP friends do not like to hear: the CCP of today is not a regime that will collapse on its own tomorrow; it still possesses very strong resilience. China has massive state-owned banks, large state-owned enterprises, capital. controls, high domestic savings, world-class manufacturing, and enormous export capacity. The CCP authorities can also delay the outbreak of many problems through bond issuance, debt restructuring, financial support, fiscal transfers, and state-owned bank rollovers. Therefore, China is not exactly the same as many small emerging countries that rely on foreign dollar loans; it is not the case that if foreign capital stops lending tomorrow, China will go bankrupt the day after. This is also why the IMF's judgment on China is that the economy remains resilient, but it must address real. estate, local debt, and domestic demand structural issues, rather than declaring that China is about to collapse. So, if someone asks me today, if the Chinese economy continues like this, will the CCP fall next year? My answer would be very direct: it cannot be foreseen at the moment. On the contrary, China's most likely future may turn out to be quite boring, and the first—and perhaps most common—scenario is long-term low growth. China hasn't collapsed, nor has the CCP fallen, but the era of high-speed growth is over. Housing prices are slowly correcting, the. population is aging, youth are becoming more conservative, people are afraid to spend, and businesses are afraid to invest. Society has entered a state where people won't starve, but they no longer believe things will necessarily get better—a situation that could drag on for ten or twenty years. The second scenario is that the worse the economy gets, the tighter the politics become, with Beijing pouring more resources into national security, stability maintenance , the military, ideology, and nationalism. The result is not that poverty leads to democracy, but rather that poverty leads to more isolation. The third scenario is the truly dangerous one: a real estate crisis, a local debt crisis, a financial crisis, mass unemployment, external war or sanctions, internal power struggles within the CCP, large-scale protests, or even issues with military loyalty, all colliding at roughly the same time. If that were to happen, it wouldn't just be an ordinary economic recession; it would be a regime crisis. So, if someone tells you in the future that China's GDP is down to 3%and the CCP is about to collapse, I suggest you look at seven things: first, are local governments. defaulting on payroll long-term? Second , have bank problems spread from isolated cases to a systemic crisis? Third, has the real estate crisis spread to core financial institutions? Fourth, are protests beginning to link up across cities and provinces? Fifth, have local governments begun to openly resist the central government? Sixth, has an open and irreconcilable split emerged among the top CCP leadership? And seventh, most importantly, have the military, armed police, or public.

security forces shown signs of deviating from central orders? If China's GDP drops to 2%, but none of these latter conditions are met, I would not say the CCP is about to collapse. Conversely, if China's GDP is still at 5 %, but the fifth, sixth, and seventh conditions occur simultaneously, I would actually find it very dangerous. Because the collapse of a regime is never just an economic problem; in the end, it inevitably becomes a political one. Now we can answer the question from the beginning of the video: if China's. economy continues to slide, will the CCP really collapse? My answer is not necessarily; even if economic growth keeps slowing, it likely won't collapse immediately. But will a long-term recession weaken the CCP? The answer is yes. It will slowly erode local government finances, the confidence of the middle class, the future outlook of the youth, the investment intentions of entrepreneurs, and the legitimacy of the CCP's rule, which was built on economic performance since the Reform and Opening-up. So, an economic crisis is not the "off" switch. for the CCP's downfall; it is more like constantly pouring gasoline into a room . The gasoline piles up and the smell gets stronger, but without a spark, the house won't burn. The real sparks might be a major financial crisis, a diplomatic or military disaster, the sudden incapacitation of top leadership , infighting within the Party, large-scale mass movements, or the military and police refusing to obey orders. If this entire chain of events were to actually trigger, that would be the moment the CCP faces true danger. But in the end, there is one very. important thing I want to discuss. I have long supported the democratization of China and hope that one day the CCP’s one-party dictatorship will come to an end, but I have never believed that Chinese people must be impoverished to the point of starvation to be worthy of freedom. Sometimes, when people see the poor state of China’s economy online, they cheer, "Let housing prices fall further, let unemployment rise higher, let the economy collapse as soon as possible, so the CCP falls faster." But do not forget, if the mainland economy truly collapses, the first people to suffer will not be the. members of the Politburo Standing Committee. The first to default on mortgages will be ordinary families, the first to lose jobs will be workers and youth, the first to go bankrupt will be small businesses, and the first to worry about their retirement will be the elderly. So, if the prerequisite for the mainland’s democratization is that over a billion people must first plunge into disaster alongside the CCP, I do not believe this is a path worth looking forward to, because the Three Principles of the People has never meant destroying the mainland to start over. This is why I feel that the Three Principles of the. People, as taught by our Founding Father Sun Yat-sen, still offers a very important reminder today: because the Three Principles are not just about civil rights, they also include nationalism and the people’s livelihood . If the mainland’s economy is incredibly strong but the people can never decide who governs them, then civil rights are not realized. But if gaining civil rights first causes the country to fall into famine, civil war, and economic collapse, then the people’s livelihood is not realized either. Therefore, the democratic transition of China I envision has never been about smashing the mainland to pieces and rebuilding from the ruins. The truly. ideal path should be, while the country is still operating normally, to gradually nationalize the military, make the judiciary truly independent, allow freedom of the press, enable local self-governance, ensure fair competition among political parties, and finally, let the people use their ballots to decide who governs the central government. That is what we call a peaceful transition. So, at most, an economic crisis in the mainland can only open a door of history . It can create cracks in an otherwise.

rigid system, allow the ruling elite to start rethinking, and enable the people to begin asking whether we can truly continue on with this system. But after that door opens, will what walks through be democracy, or just another dictator? Will what walks through be constitutional government, or warlordism? Whether we walk into a free China or yet another dynastic cycle is not something that GDP figures can decide for us. Ultimately, it depends on whether the people of the mainland have organization , a civil society, new political forces. , and a system that allows different parties to compete peacefully rather than killing each other with guns. This is where I believe the National Revolution remains truly unfinished. It is not about waiting for over a billion people to go down with the regime, nor is it about hoping for another era of chaos. It is about one day returning the power that belongs to the people, without the need for famine, civil war, or the slaughter of tens of millions. An economic crisis could be fuel, or it could be the power that opens the door to history. But whether we can turn an economic crisis into a transition toward freedom ultimately depends on the people. So one day, if the CCP truly reaches a historical turning point due to prolonged economic, political, and social crises, I hope the mainland will not usher in another dynastic cycle, but rather truly complete the civil rights revolution that began over 100 years ago with the Xinhai Revolution. This road may still be very long, and the CCP will certainly not exit the stage of history just because of a year or two of poor GDP. But as long as the desire of the Chinese people for freedom , democracy, and a republic remains, the political cause of the National Revolution will not vanish due to economic prosperity, nor will it cease due to political repression. The political cause of the National Revolution may be arduous, but it will never end. Alright, that is where we will end our story for today. If you enjoyed this episode, please help us by clicking subscribe and sharing it. We are also incredibly grateful to those who are able to join as members. Additionally, our Discord and Telegram. groups are now open, where you can receive our updates in real-time, and we welcome everyone to join in the conversation. That is all for today’s study notes. We will see you next time, bye-bye.

摘要

民族團結立法與自治的疑問

影片開頭，阿牛談到2026年7月中國新施行的《民族團結進步促進法》。他指出，第15條規定學校以國家通用語言作為基本教學語言，同時表示尊重並保障少數民族語言的學習與使用；第46條要求宗教團體與場所增進中華民族共同體意識，並堅持宗教中國化。阿牛認為更值得注意的是第20條：父母或監護人須教育未成年人熱愛中國共產黨、祖國、人民與中華民族，並不得灌輸有損民族團結進步的觀念。他因此追問，禁止族群歧視與要求家庭培養對執政黨的愛，是否真是同一種平等保障？

接著，影片插入一段宣傳內容，介紹以中華民國地圖與旗幟為主題的周邊商品。之後阿牛提出本集主題：既然西藏名義上已是自治區，也有地方政府、人民代表大會與民族自治法律，為何仍有人長期要求真正的自治？他將問題延伸為：一個國家應靠讓所有人變得相同來維持統一，還是能建立制度，使不同群體和平共處？

自治的關鍵：誰能作決定

阿牛以新北市的日常治理作對照：居民可以透過民意代表反映交通問題、要求說明教育預算，也能用選票更換表現不佳的市長。這些權利背後的前提，是居民可以參與並影響地方公共事務。轉到西藏，教學應使用多少藏語、文化經費如何分配、寺院如何傳承教育，以及地方最高政治領導人由誰決定，才是自治的實質問題。自治不只是地圖上的不同顏色或掛上「自治政府」的牌子，而是地方能否自行作決策，並在權利受侵害時尋求救濟。

阿牛承認，中國確有法定的民族區域自治框架。1984年《民族區域自治法》規定自治區主席須由實行區域自治的民族公民擔任，也允許制定地方性法規；地方若認為上級指示不符合當地情況，也可申請調整。然而，地方規章往往仍須上級批准，重要政治方向也受中國共產黨領導所限制。即使藏族人士擔任自治區主席，居民仍無法像台灣選舉地方首長那樣，透過自由競爭的選舉決定最高政治領導人。

他進一步提醒，少數民族官員的存在本身並不足以證明權力已經共享。阿牛引述一項2025年研究：研究分析2010年至2024年的藏族官員資料，發現藏族人士雖在部分諮詢機構占有一定席次，但在具有實質影響力的黨政機構中的代表性有所下降。這項研究並非主張沒有藏族官員，而是提醒觀眾應追問：誰掌握最後的決策權？阿牛認為，判斷自治不能只看它是否存在，更要看自治程度、地方能否自主行事，以及是否有獨立而有效的救濟機制。

1946年憲法中的西藏自治承諾

為理解西藏自治制度的歷史脈絡，阿牛將時間帶回1946年。抗日戰爭結束後，國共衝突再起，當時的中華民國國民大會在南京通過《中華民國憲法》，並於次年施行。除了常被提及的五權憲法與中央政府體制，阿牛特別關注憲法中的地方自治與族群條文：第5條規定各民族一律平等，第119條提到蒙古各盟旗地方自治制度由法律制定，而第120條則明文指出：「西藏自治制度，應予以保障。」

阿牛認為，「保障」一詞顯示制憲者並未將西藏視作一般地方行政單位，而是在憲法中承認其特殊性，並認為應受到保護。憲法第168條也提及保障邊疆各民族地位，第169條則談到扶助其教育、文化與社會事業。這些條文呈現一種構想：不同民族與地區可以共享憲政架構，卻不必一律採取完全相同的制度。

不過，阿牛提醒，不能因此認定1946年的憲法已經解決西藏問題。當時中華民國中央政府對西藏缺乏完整的實際治理能力，各方對西藏的歷史與政治地位也存在重大分歧；第120條雖承諾保障自治，卻沒有說明自治政府如何組成、教育文化與宗教領域享有何種權限，或中央違反承諾時西藏可以向誰申訴。換言之，憲法提出了值得重視的原則，卻還不是一套能實際執行的完整制度。

他以公司章程作比喻：只寫下保障員工參與決策，並沒有回答員工能參與哪些決策、投票是否有法律效力，以及管理層忽視意見時該怎麼辦。阿牛也特別說明，《中華民國憲法》如今在台灣具有實際運作範圍，不能只因歷史文本曾寫下西藏自治，就推論該條文已直接實現，或決定了今日西藏的法律與政治安排。這段歷史真正留下的問題是：民族自治能否成為受憲法保障、政府不能任意撤回的制度？

轉向1951年的協議

影片最後指出，1946年之後，西藏自治與宗教保障的承諾並未消失。中國共產黨於1949年成立，人民解放軍於1950年進入西藏地區作戰；到了1951年，中共與西藏代表又起草了一份重要文件，當中同樣涉及自治與宗教保障。阿牛以「承諾不斷出現，衝突為何反而加深」作為後續探討的引子，但影片字幕在介紹《十七條協議》簽署之際中斷，尚未展開後續分析。

值得閱讀的理由

  • 從西藏自治的歷史與制度出發，拆解「有自治之名」與「能自主決策」之間的差距。
  • 串連1946年《中華民國憲法》與1951年《十七條協議》，呈現自治承諾如何在不同時期出現。
  • 以台灣地方民主的日常經驗作對照，讓自治、代表性與問責等抽象概念更容易理解。
  • 提出值得深思的核心問題：國家團結是否必須建立在同化之上，還是能透過保障差異來實現共存？

摘要

民族團結立法與自治的疑問

影片開頭，阿牛談到2026年7月中國新施行的《民族團結進步促進法》。他指出，第15條規定學校以國家通用語言作為基本教學語言，同時表示尊重並保障少數民族語言的學習與使用；第46條要求宗教團體與場所增進中華民族共同體意識，並堅持宗教中國化。阿牛認為更值得注意的是第20條：父母或監護人須教育未成年人熱愛中國共產黨、祖國、人民與中華民族，並不得灌輸有損民族團結進步的觀念。他因此追問，禁止族群歧視與要求家庭培養對執政黨的愛，是否真是同一種平等保障？

接著，影片插入一段宣傳內容，介紹以中華民國地圖與旗幟為主題的周邊商品。之後阿牛提出本集主題：既然西藏名義上已是自治區，也有地方政府、人民代表大會與民族自治法律，為何仍有人長期要求真正的自治？他將問題延伸為：一個國家應靠讓所有人變得相同來維持統一，還是能建立制度，使不同群體和平共處？

自治的關鍵：誰能作決定

阿牛以新北市的日常治理作對照：居民可以透過民意代表反映交通問題、要求說明教育預算，也能用選票更換表現不佳的市長。這些權利背後的前提，是居民可以參與並影響地方公共事務。轉到西藏，教學應使用多少藏語、文化經費如何分配、寺院如何傳承教育，以及地方最高政治領導人由誰決定，才是自治的實質問題。自治不只是地圖上的不同顏色或掛上「自治政府」的牌子，而是地方能否自行作決策，並在權利受侵害時尋求救濟。

阿牛承認，中國確有法定的民族區域自治框架。1984年《民族區域自治法》規定自治區主席須由實行區域自治的民族公民擔任，也允許制定地方性法規；地方若認為上級指示不符合當地情況，也可申請調整。然而，地方規章往往仍須上級批准，重要政治方向也受中國共產黨領導所限制。即使藏族人士擔任自治區主席，居民仍無法像台灣選舉地方首長那樣，透過自由競爭的選舉決定最高政治領導人。

他進一步提醒，少數民族官員的存在本身並不足以證明權力已經共享。阿牛引述一項2025年研究：研究分析2010年至2024年的藏族官員資料，發現藏族人士雖在部分諮詢機構占有一定席次，但在具有實質影響力的黨政機構中的代表性有所下降。這項研究並非主張沒有藏族官員，而是提醒觀眾應追問：誰掌握最後的決策權？阿牛認為，判斷自治不能只看它是否存在，更要看自治程度、地方能否自主行事，以及是否有獨立而有效的救濟機制。

1946年憲法中的西藏自治承諾

為理解西藏自治制度的歷史脈絡，阿牛將時間帶回1946年。抗日戰爭結束後，國共衝突再起，當時的中華民國國民大會在南京通過《中華民國憲法》，並於次年施行。除了常被提及的五權憲法與中央政府體制，阿牛特別關注憲法中的地方自治與族群條文：第5條規定各民族一律平等，第119條提到蒙古各盟旗地方自治制度由法律制定，而第120條則明文指出：「西藏自治制度，應予以保障。」

阿牛認為，「保障」一詞顯示制憲者並未將西藏視作一般地方行政單位，而是在憲法中承認其特殊性，並認為應受到保護。憲法第168條也提及保障邊疆各民族地位，第169條則談到扶助其教育、文化與社會事業。這些條文呈現一種構想：不同民族與地區可以共享憲政架構，卻不必一律採取完全相同的制度。

不過，阿牛提醒，不能因此認定1946年的憲法已經解決西藏問題。當時中華民國中央政府對西藏缺乏完整的實際治理能力，各方對西藏的歷史與政治地位也存在重大分歧；第120條雖承諾保障自治，卻沒有說明自治政府如何組成、教育文化與宗教領域享有何種權限，或中央違反承諾時西藏可以向誰申訴。換言之，憲法提出了值得重視的原則，卻還不是一套能實際執行的完整制度。

他以公司章程作比喻：只寫下保障員工參與決策，並沒有回答員工能參與哪些決策、投票是否有法律效力，以及管理層忽視意見時該怎麼辦。阿牛也特別說明，《中華民國憲法》如今在台灣具有實際運作範圍，不能只因歷史文本曾寫下西藏自治，就推論該條文已直接實現，或決定了今日西藏的法律與政治安排。這段歷史真正留下的問題是：民族自治能否成為受憲法保障、政府不能任意撤回的制度？

轉向1951年的協議

影片最後指出，1946年之後，西藏自治與宗教保障的承諾並未消失。中國共產黨於1949年成立，人民解放軍於1950年進入西藏地區作戰；到了1951年，中共與西藏代表又起草了一份重要文件，當中同樣涉及自治與宗教保障。阿牛以「承諾不斷出現，衝突為何反而加深」作為後續探討的引子，但影片字幕在介紹《十七條協議》簽署之際中斷，尚未展開後續分析。

================================================

In July 2026, the PRC's newly implemented Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress sparked new controversy. Article 15 requires schools to use the national common language as the basic medium for instruction, while simultaneously pledging to respect and protect the learning and use of minority languages. Article 46 requires religious groups, institutions, and venues to promote the awareness of a shared Chinese national identity and insist on the Sinicization of religion. But what surprised me most wasn't these two articles. It was Article 20, which explicitly. mandates that parents or other guardians must educate and guide minors to love the Chinese Communist Party, love the motherland, love the people, and love the Chinese nation, and forbids them from instilling ideas that are detrimental to ethnic unity and progress . Think about it, everyone. It's understandable for the government to forbid discrimination against other ethnic groups, but is requiring parents to guide their children to love a ruling party the same thing as guaranteeing equality? >> People often ask about the map in my background. Today, I’ll start with a question for. you all: In mainland China, there is a region with "autonomous" right in its name, which has a local government, a People's Congress, and even specific laws for ethnic autonomy, yet some of its people have long demanded true autonomy. Why is that? That’s right, we are talking about Tibet. You might think, since autonomy has been established for decades, what is there left to fight for? Is it because the demands for autonomy never come to an end? Or does this system harbor a. contradiction from the very beginning? Even stranger, as early as 80 years ago , Article 120 of the 1946 Constitution of the Republic of China already stated that the autonomous system of Tibet shall be guaranteed. If autonomy was promised 80 years ago, why is there still such a huge controversy today? Furthermore, in 1951, the CCP and Tibetan representatives signed the Seventeen-Point Agreement, which also included a promise of regional ethnic autonomy. Since autonomy has appeared. more than once in history, where exactly does the problem lie? Today, we are not just discussing Tibetan history; we are addressing a bigger question: should a country maintain unity by making everyone the same, or by creating a system where diverse people can live in peace? Finally, we must answer whether the Tibet issue would naturally resolve if China were to truly democratize one day . Imagine living in New Taipei City today. . If you're unhappy with traffic, you can ask a councilor for improvements. If you feel school resources are unfairly distributed, you can demand the city explain its budget. If the mayor performs poorly, you can vote them out. These seem mundane, but they rely on a vital premise: local residents have the right to participate in and influence their own public affairs. Now, shift the scene to Tibet: how much Tibetan language should be taught in.

schools? How should local cultural funds be allocated? How can monasteries pass on traditional education? Who decides the region’s top political leader? And when the central and local governments clash, who has the final say ? These questions are the true substance of autonomy. Autonomy isn't just coloring a map differently or hanging a sign that says "Autonomous People's Government." To be fair, China isn't entirely without. such frameworks; the 1984 Law on Regional Ethnic Autonomy mandates that the head of an autonomous region must be from that ethnic group and allows for local regulations. When higher-level directives don't fit local realities, there is even a process to request adjustments. So, it is inaccurate to say China's ethnic autonomy doesn't exist legally. However, the problem is that local regulations often require higher-level approval, and important political directions are constrained by the. Communist Party’s leadership. Even if a Tibetan holds the position of regional chair, local residents cannot determine the highest political leadership through free, competitive elections like those for county mayors in Taiwan. You might ask, doesn't appointing more Tibetan officials count as a form of protection? It certainly has symbolic significance, but it is not enough. I often feel that for the word " autonomy," the most important question isn't whether it exists, but to what extent? Can one make decisions for. oneself? When rights are infringed upon , is there a way to seek redress? If local government powers are difficult to exercise without central approval and there is no truly independent mechanism for relief, this "autonomy" is hard to trust. However, this system did not emerge overnight. To understand why Tibet is where it is today, we must travel back to a time before the current autonomous region, to 1946. Shortly after the Second Sino-Japanese War, the conflict between the KMT and. the CCP escalated again. Article 5 stipulates that "all groups shall be equal," and Article 119 states that " the local self-government system of the various Mongolian leagues shall be. determined by law." Then, Article 120 features a very special sentence: "The self-government system of Tibet shall be guaranteed." I find the term " guaranteed" to be the most intriguing part. This sentence tells us, at the very least, that the drafters of the Constitution did not view Tibet as just an ordinary local administrative unit. Furthermore, Article 168 of the Constitution mentions guaranteeing the status of the various ethnic groups.

in border regions, while Article 169 discusses support for their education, culture, and social enterprises. First, the central government of the Republic of China at the time lacked complete, practical governing power over Tibet, and there were major disagreements among all parties regarding Tibet's historical and political status. In other words , while the Constitution established a principle worthy of attention, it was not yet a complete, implementable system. . It’s like writing "guaranteeing employee participation in decision-making" in a company’s articles of incorporation; everyone is happy to hear it, but what comes next? You see, autonomy, religion, existing systems, and reform procedures were all. written into the 1951 agreement. This makes the historical contradiction even more worth questioning: with so many promises made, why do many Tibetans today still believe that true autonomy was never realized? You can think of this agreement as an arrangement written by both sides for their future life together. The central government had requirements concerning national defense, foreign affairs, and national unification, while the Tibetan side cared about their existing political system, religious culture, and local affairs. The problem is that merely writing.

different demands on a piece of paper does not mean that trust has been truly established, especially when the military and political power held by the two sides is unequal. Whether promises can be verified and honored becomes critically important. First, the agreement itself is subject to significant controversy. The CCP views it as a major achievement of peaceful liberation, while the Dalai Lama's side argues that it was reached under unequal conditions and duress. Even regarding whether this agreement was signed with genuine, free consent,. the narratives of both sides differ. Furthermore, how the promises are implemented is far more important than how elegantly they are written. When the central and local governments differ over the pace of reform, political rights, and religious activities, is there a mutually accepted procedure to prevent the conflict from escalating? In 1956, the CCP Central Committee established the Preparatory Committee for the Tibet Autonomous Region, and new party arrangements gradually took hold locally. As the situation evolved, tensions across Tibetan regions regarding reforms,. military deployment, and political control gradually accumulated. In 1959, a major conflict erupted in Lhasa, and the Dalai Lama left Tibet for India. The Chinese authorities and the Tibetan exile community offer completely different interpretations of the causes , responsibilities, and nature of the event. In 1965, the Tibet Autonomous Region was officially established. You may have noticed a thought-provoking aspect of this historical process: there was a promise of autonomy in 1951, and the establishment of an autonomous region in 1965, but the most critical question never disappeared—how much real. decision-making power do local residents actually have over their political, religious, and cultural lives? We must avoid a simplistic narrative here, such as attributing decades of complex conflict to a single document or event, but we also cannot assume that the mere establishment of an autonomous region automatically puts previous controversies to rest. Imagine a Tibetan child who grows up speaking the language at home, with parents telling family stories in Tibetan, but once they enter school, the main curriculum relies increasingly on Mandarin. They learn to communicate with people from other regions, but may gradually. lose the ability to read and understand history in their mother tongue. This is not to say that this happens in every Tibetan household, but in May 2020 , Human Rights Watch published a study analyzing preschool education policies in Tibetan areas and the potential impact of Mandarin becoming the primary language of instruction on the transmission of the Tibetan language. The report uses research on official documents and limited interviews; while it cannot represent every family, it highlights risks that are worth tracking . I want to be clear: there is nothing. wrong with learning Mandarin. A common language helps with education, work, and communication between different ethnic groups, but the question is: why must learning Mandarin compete with preserving the Tibetan language? Take the example of Taiwan: if one day Taiwanese, Hakka, and Indigenous languages were restricted to very little class time, and the government said, " It doesn't matter, just speak them at home." Would we worry that the next generation would become increasingly unable to read or write their mother tongue? Because language is more than just speech; it contains stories,.

classic songs, and the ways our ancestors understood the world. Culture is not just items on display in a museum ; it requires living people to continue using it. Next, let’s look at religion. For many Tibetans, Tibetan Buddhism is not just a faith, but a part of their culture, philosophy, and community life . Willingness to comply with laws and public safety regulations is certainly reasonable, but how is religious education to be passed down? To what extent should the government be allowed to intervene? This question has sparked a new debate following the "Law on. Promoting National Unity and Progress" implemented by the CCP in July 2026. Article 15 mandates that schools use the national common language and script as the basic medium for education, while also pledging to respect and protect the learning and use of minority languages. Article 46 requires religious groups, institutions, and venues to promote the shared consciousness of the Chinese nation and adhere to the Sinicization of religion. What surprises me most, however, is not these two articles, but Article 20,. which explicitly mandates that parents or other guardians must guide minors to love the Communist Party of China, the motherland, the people, and the Chinese nation, and must not instill ideas detrimental to ethnic unity and progress . Think about it: the government asking you not to discriminate against other ethnic groups is understandable, but requiring parents to guide children to love a ruling party—is that the same thing as ensuring equality? Of course, we cannot conclude that any family discussing a different history. will necessarily be punished just because this law exists; we still have to look at the actual implementation and specific cases. But if people cannot predict whether peacefully discussing ethnic history or autonomy will be interpreted as detrimental to national unity, it easily creates a pressure that discourages them from speaking out. I also want to remind everyone that when discussing these laws, we must distinguish three layers: the text of the law itself is the first, how the government actually enforces it is the second, and the impact it has on. children, families, or religious communities is the third. We cannot judge every family's experience solely based on the text of a law, nor can we ignore the actual outcomes just by looking at the official stated intentions. From the official perspective, promoting a common language and emphasizing national identity is intended to foster communication and reduce differences, and the government also highlights achievements in Tibet's infrastructure, healthcare, education, and economy— these results should be evaluated fairly based on concrete data. However, I want. to separate two things: the government helping to build schools is a public construction project, but whether you can participate in deciding how schools teach is a matter of autonomy. No matter how well-paved the roads are, they do not automatically answer the question of whether the people have a political choice. So, as we look from the 1946 Constitution and the 1951 Agreement to the new laws of 2026, we find the same question recurring: is the state protecting the coexistence of different cultures, or is it demanding that different cultures converge into a single political identity? Must the future of Tibet be a choice between only two options: independence or accepting the current system? In fact, the Dalai Lama once proposed a different political approach. Many people, upon hearing about the Tibet issue, assume it must be a choice between independence or unification. However, the "Middle Way" proposed by the 14th Dalai Lama does not set independence as the goal; instead, it advocates for genuine autonomy within the framework of the People's Republic of China through peaceful negotiation.

This proposal hopes that Tibetans can enjoy greater autonomy in matters such as culture, religion, education, and environmental protection. Local legislation and administration should also have mechanisms for democratic election, while national defense and foreign affairs remain the responsibility of the central government . This does not mean all Tibetans agree with this plan; some support genuine autonomy, while others advocate for independence. The CCP authorities also have their own opposition to the "Middle Way" and have not accepted this set of arrangements,. so we cannot package it as a universally agreed-upon answer. What is truly worth noting is that it turns abstract political disagreements into institutional issues that can be discussed concretely, such as who decides on education and how the local autonomous assemblies are formed. Under legal protection, how much autonomy is there exactly? When there is a conflict between the central government and the local region, is it decided by an independent court, or is it ultimately determined by political power? Sometimes the most difficult part of a political dispute is not that someone is being unreasonable, but that. both sides may have completely different understandings of history and sovereignty. If you demand that the other side first acknowledge your entire historical view before discussing institutions, then I fear negotiations will never proceed. But if we start with what rights and procedures are needed to live together, at least we can identify the specific content that needs to be negotiated. Of course, this does not mean that talking only about education and culture can avoid all sovereignty disputes, nor does it mean we can decide the future for Tibetans without asking for their own will. The most basic prerequisite for genuine autonomy is giving the people involved the right to participate in the choice, and this brings us to the final question : if China were to democratize in the future, would the autonomy of Tibet be guaranteed? Over the years, I have participated in many discussions on China's democratization. People discuss whether to adopt a presidential, parliamentary, or federal system in the future, and some even suggest re-examining the 1946 Constitution of the Republic of China. But I often wonder, even if the mainland. were to hold free elections one day, would the Tibet issue be automatically resolved? Suppose there is a democratically elected parliament in a future China, and the majority passes a law requiring every region to use the exact same language and education system, but Tibetans feel this impacts their culture . In that case, can the majority simply say, "We have more votes, so you must comply"? I believe it cannot be that simple, because democracy is not just about majority rule; it must also protect the fundamental rights of minorities. If ninety percent of people. vote to restrict a certain religion, does that restriction automatically conform to human rights protections? Of course not. Therefore, a constitution should not only grant the government legitimate authority but also tell the government what it cannot do, even if it has majority support. Regarding ethnic autonomy, I believe it must answer at least a few questions: can the autonomous region's assembly and government be truly elected by the local residents? How much governing authority exists over education, culture, and local affairs? Can the central. government unilaterally take that authority back? When disputes arise, can the people seek relief through an independent judicial mechanism? At the same time, autonomy cannot become a privilege for a single ethnic group; Tibet is not just inhabited by one group , but also by other residents. Guaranteeing one group's cultural and political participation does not mean that the basic rights of other ethnicities or individuals can be ignored. This is why I keep emphasizing constitutionalism, rather than just elections. The spirit of constitutionalism is to allow different groups to live under a system where power is limited, preventing whoever has the majority.

today from deciding the fate of others tomorrow. However, no matter how well a system is designed, it may not function well if the people do not understand it. Will local assembly members actually audit the budget? Do the people know how to oversee the government? When disputes occur between different ethnic groups, is everyone willing to resolve them through legal and democratic procedures? This is why I have dedicated myself to distributing civic textbooks; I hope that people don't just learn to shout about democracy, but understand how power, the rule of law, and public participation. actually work. Of course, there is another easily overlooked issue: some people may identify as Tibetan while also being willing to participate in a larger political community, while others may have completely different thoughts. These identities may not necessarily be covered by a single standard answer; a truly capable system does not need to dictate thoughts for everyone beforehand , yet can still protect each other's rights. When we re-examine Article 120 of the 1946 Constitution, we become clearer about its value and its limitations. It left behind constitutional principles worth studying, but true autonomy still requires democratic participation, specific legal protections, and a willingness to negotiate. Returning to the question at the very beginning: Tibet is named an autonomous region, so why do some still demand true autonomy? Because autonomy is not just a sign hung on a wall, nor is it whatever the government says it is. True autonomy means giving local people the right to participate in their own public affairs , such that even if the central government disagrees, these rights remain protected by the constitution and. the law. The 1946 Constitution of the Republic of China stated: "The system of self-government in Tibet shall be safeguarded." The 17-Point Agreement of 1951 also once promised autonomy, but history tells us that without a system for real implementation, even the most beautiful political promises can end up as just a piece of paper. This reminds me of the Three Principles of the People and the core political ideals of the National Revolution proposed by Dr. Sun Yat-sen back then. Nationalism should not be about demanding that all ethnic groups abandon their own cultures and identities, but about allowing different. peoples to build a political community together based on equality, freedom, and mutual respect. The Principle of Democracy is certainly not about letting a small group of power-holders decide the fate of the people, but about enabling the people to truly participate in politics, oversee the government, and have systems that safeguard their rights . As for the Principle of the People's Livelihood, it reminds us that the ultimate purpose of any political system is to ensure that every one of us can live a life with dignity and security. Therefore, I have always believed that the true meaning of the National Revolution was never just to overthrow a. regime, but more importantly, to build a nation that is free, equal, democratic, and where power is constrained by a constitution. If mainland China ever undergoes a democratic transition, we cannot simply replace one authoritarian government with another; instead, we must allow people of different ethnic groups to truly become masters of their own destiny. This is why I believe the Three Principles of the People and the constitutional democracy of the Republic of China remain worthy of our continued study, practice, and pursuit today. The path of the National Revolution is fraught with thousands of hardships, but it will never cease. Alright, that is. where we end today’s story. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 從西藏自治的歷史與制度出發，拆解「有自治之名」與「能自主決策」之間的差距。
  • 串連1946年《中華民國憲法》與1951年《十七條協議》，呈現自治承諾如何在不同時期出現。
  • 以台灣地方民主的日常經驗作對照，讓自治、代表性與問責等抽象概念更容易理解。
  • 提出值得深思的核心問題：國家團結是否必須建立在同化之上，還是能透過保障差異來實現共存？

摘要

民族團結立法與自治的疑問

影片開頭，阿牛談到2026年7月中國新施行的《民族團結進步促進法》。他指出，第15條規定學校以國家通用語言作為基本教學語言，同時表示尊重並保障少數民族語言的學習與使用；第46條要求宗教團體與場所增進中華民族共同體意識，並堅持宗教中國化。阿牛認為更值得注意的是第20條：父母或監護人須教育未成年人熱愛中國共產黨、祖國、人民與中華民族，並不得灌輸有損民族團結進步的觀念。他因此追問，禁止族群歧視與要求家庭培養對執政黨的愛，是否真是同一種平等保障？

接著，影片插入一段宣傳內容，介紹以中華民國地圖與旗幟為主題的周邊商品。之後阿牛提出本集主題：既然西藏名義上已是自治區，也有地方政府、人民代表大會與民族自治法律，為何仍有人長期要求真正的自治？他將問題延伸為：一個國家應靠讓所有人變得相同來維持統一，還是能建立制度，使不同群體和平共處？

自治的關鍵：誰能作決定

阿牛以新北市的日常治理作對照：居民可以透過民意代表反映交通問題、要求說明教育預算，也能用選票更換表現不佳的市長。這些權利背後的前提，是居民可以參與並影響地方公共事務。轉到西藏，教學應使用多少藏語、文化經費如何分配、寺院如何傳承教育，以及地方最高政治領導人由誰決定，才是自治的實質問題。自治不只是地圖上的不同顏色或掛上「自治政府」的牌子，而是地方能否自行作決策，並在權利受侵害時尋求救濟。

阿牛承認，中國確有法定的民族區域自治框架。1984年《民族區域自治法》規定自治區主席須由實行區域自治的民族公民擔任，也允許制定地方性法規；地方若認為上級指示不符合當地情況，也可申請調整。然而，地方規章往往仍須上級批准，重要政治方向也受中國共產黨領導所限制。即使藏族人士擔任自治區主席，居民仍無法像台灣選舉地方首長那樣，透過自由競爭的選舉決定最高政治領導人。

他進一步提醒，少數民族官員的存在本身並不足以證明權力已經共享。阿牛引述一項2025年研究：研究分析2010年至2024年的藏族官員資料，發現藏族人士雖在部分諮詢機構占有一定席次，但在具有實質影響力的黨政機構中的代表性有所下降。這項研究並非主張沒有藏族官員，而是提醒觀眾應追問：誰掌握最後的決策權？阿牛認為，判斷自治不能只看它是否存在，更要看自治程度、地方能否自主行事，以及是否有獨立而有效的救濟機制。

1946年憲法中的西藏自治承諾

為理解西藏自治制度的歷史脈絡，阿牛將時間帶回1946年。抗日戰爭結束後，國共衝突再起，當時的中華民國國民大會在南京通過《中華民國憲法》，並於次年施行。除了常被提及的五權憲法與中央政府體制，阿牛特別關注憲法中的地方自治與族群條文：第5條規定各民族一律平等，第119條提到蒙古各盟旗地方自治制度由法律制定，而第120條則明文指出：「西藏自治制度，應予以保障。」

阿牛認為，「保障」一詞顯示制憲者並未將西藏視作一般地方行政單位，而是在憲法中承認其特殊性，並認為應受到保護。憲法第168條也提及保障邊疆各民族地位，第169條則談到扶助其教育、文化與社會事業。這些條文呈現一種構想：不同民族與地區可以共享憲政架構，卻不必一律採取完全相同的制度。

不過，阿牛提醒，不能因此認定1946年的憲法已經解決西藏問題。當時中華民國中央政府對西藏缺乏完整的實際治理能力，各方對西藏的歷史與政治地位也存在重大分歧；第120條雖承諾保障自治，卻沒有說明自治政府如何組成、教育文化與宗教領域享有何種權限，或中央違反承諾時西藏可以向誰申訴。換言之，憲法提出了值得重視的原則，卻還不是一套能實際執行的完整制度。

他以公司章程作比喻：只寫下保障員工參與決策，並沒有回答員工能參與哪些決策、投票是否有法律效力，以及管理層忽視意見時該怎麼辦。阿牛也特別說明，《中華民國憲法》如今在台灣具有實際運作範圍，不能只因歷史文本曾寫下西藏自治，就推論該條文已直接實現，或決定了今日西藏的法律與政治安排。這段歷史真正留下的問題是：民族自治能否成為受憲法保障、政府不能任意撤回的制度？

轉向1951年的協議

影片最後指出，1946年之後，西藏自治與宗教保障的承諾並未消失。中國共產黨於1949年成立，人民解放軍於1950年進入西藏地區作戰；到了1951年，中共與西藏代表又起草了一份重要文件，當中同樣涉及自治與宗教保障。阿牛以「承諾不斷出現，衝突為何反而加深」作為後續探討的引子，但影片字幕在介紹《十七條協議》簽署之際中斷，尚未展開後續分析。

schools? How should local cultural funds be allocated? How can monasteries pass on traditional education? Who decides the region’s top political leader? And when the central and local governments clash, who has the final say ? These questions are the true substance of autonomy. Autonomy isn't just coloring a map differently or hanging a sign that says "Autonomous People's Government." To be fair, China isn't entirely without. such frameworks; the 1984 Law on Regional Ethnic Autonomy mandates that the head of an autonomous region must be from that ethnic group and allows for local regulations. When higher-level directives don't fit local realities, there is even a process to request adjustments. So, it is inaccurate to say China's ethnic autonomy doesn't exist legally. However, the problem is that local regulations often require higher-level approval, and important political directions are constrained by the. Communist Party’s leadership. Even if a Tibetan holds the position of regional chair, local residents cannot determine the highest political leadership through free, competitive elections like those for county mayors in Taiwan. You might ask, doesn't appointing more Tibetan officials count as a form of protection? It certainly has symbolic significance, but it is not enough. In 2025, scholars analyzed data on Tibetan officials from 2010 to 2024 and. found that while Tibetans hold a significant proportion of seats in certain advisory bodies, their representation in genuinely influential party and government institutions has declined. Note that this study doesn't claim there are no Tibetan officials; it reminds us that we shouldn't just look at an official's ethnicity, but at who holds the final decision-making power. I often feel that for the word " autonomy," the most important question isn't whether it exists, but to what extent? Can one make decisions for. oneself? When rights are infringed upon , is there a way to seek redress? If local government powers are difficult to exercise without central approval and there is no truly independent mechanism for relief, this "autonomy" is hard to trust. However, this system did not emerge overnight. To understand why Tibet is where it is today, we must travel back to a time before the current autonomous region, to 1946. Shortly after the Second Sino-Japanese War, the conflict between the KMT and. the CCP escalated again. The Republic of China convened the Constituent National Assembly in Nanjing and passed the Constitution of the Republic of China, which went into effect the following year. When most people talk about this Constitution, they think of the Five-Power Constitution, the President, the Executive Yuan, or the Legislative Yuan. But today, I want to look at something else: the rarely discussed provisions on local autonomy. Article 5 stipulates that "all groups shall be equal," and Article 119 states that " the local self-government system of the various Mongolian leagues shall be. determined by law." Then, Article 120 features a very special sentence: "The self-government system of Tibet shall be guaranteed." I find the term " guaranteed" to be the most intriguing part. This sentence tells us, at the very least, that the drafters of the Constitution did not view Tibet as just an ordinary local administrative unit. Instead, they explicitly acknowledged in the text of the Constitution that Tibet possessed a unique character requiring protection. Furthermore, Article 168 of the Constitution mentions guaranteeing the status of the various ethnic groups.

in border regions, while Article 169 discusses support for their education, culture, and social enterprises. Putting these provisions together, we see a conceptual framework where everyone can live under a shared constitutional structure, while different ethnic groups and regions do not necessarily need to have identical arrangements. But let's not rush to applaud just yet, because the audience might mistakenly believe that the Republic of China in 1946 had already solved the Tibet issue . The reality is actually far from simple. . First, the central government of the Republic of China at the time lacked complete, practical governing power over Tibet, and there were major disagreements among all parties regarding Tibet's historical and political status. Second, although Article 120 promised a "guarantee," it did not specify how the autonomous government would be formed, what autonomy it had in education, culture, or religion, or to whom Tibet could appeal if the central government violated that guarantee. In other words , while the Constitution established a principle worthy of attention, it was not yet a complete, implementable system. . It’s like writing "guaranteeing employee participation in decision-making" in a company’s articles of incorporation; everyone is happy to hear it, but what comes next? What kind of decisions can they participate in? Do their votes have legal force? What happens if management ignores them? Without these specific rules, that promise remains nothing more than words on paper. It is also important to note that the Constitution of the Republic of China has its practical scope of operation in Taiwan today. We cannot infer from reading this historical text that it directly dictates the current legal and political. arrangements for Tibet. Studying a constitutional provision and claiming that this provision has already been realized are two completely different things. Similarly, as we re-examine the 1946 Constitution today, we shouldn't deify it as a historically successful answer. Its true value lies in the question it leaves behind: can ethnic autonomy become a system protected by the constitution, one that the government cannot arbitrarily revoke? But the most compelling part is yet to come, because after 1946, promises. regarding Tibetan autonomy did not disappear. Even by 1951, another significant document was drafted, enshrining autonomy and religious protections. If promises kept appearing, why did the conflict only deepen? The CCP was founded in 1949, and the PLA entered Tibetan regions to engage in combat in 1950. By May 1951, the CCP and Tibetan representatives signed the famous 17- Point Agreement. This was not a document merely demanding submission to the central government. It contained several. clauses relevant to our discussion: Article 3 mentions the right of the Tibetan people to practice autonomy under the policy of regional ethnic autonomy; Article 4 states that the central government will not alter the existing political system of Tibet or the established status of the Dalai Lama ; Article 7 promises the protection of religious beliefs, customs, and monasteries; and Article 11 specifies that reforms should be implemented by the local Tibetan government itself, without coercion from the center. You see, autonomy, religion, existing systems, and reform procedures were all. written into the 1951 agreement. This makes the historical contradiction even more worth questioning: with so many promises made, why do many Tibetans today still believe that true autonomy was never realized? You can think of this agreement as an arrangement written by both sides for their future life together. The central government had requirements concerning national defense, foreign affairs, and national unification, while the Tibetan side cared about their existing political system, religious culture, and local affairs. The problem is that merely writing.

different demands on a piece of paper does not mean that trust has been truly established, especially when the military and political power held by the two sides is unequal. Whether promises can be verified and honored becomes critically important. First, the agreement itself is subject to significant controversy. The CCP views it as a major achievement of peaceful liberation, while the Dalai Lama's side argues that it was reached under unequal conditions and duress. Even regarding whether this agreement was signed with genuine, free consent,. the narratives of both sides differ. Furthermore, how the promises are implemented is far more important than how elegantly they are written. When the central and local governments differ over the pace of reform, political rights, and religious activities, is there a mutually accepted procedure to prevent the conflict from escalating? In 1956, the CCP Central Committee established the Preparatory Committee for the Tibet Autonomous Region, and new party arrangements gradually took hold locally. As the situation evolved, tensions across Tibetan regions regarding reforms,. military deployment, and political control gradually accumulated. In 1959, a major conflict erupted in Lhasa, and the Dalai Lama left Tibet for India. The Chinese authorities and the Tibetan exile community offer completely different interpretations of the causes , responsibilities, and nature of the event. In 1965, the Tibet Autonomous Region was officially established. You may have noticed a thought-provoking aspect of this historical process: there was a promise of autonomy in 1951, and the establishment of an autonomous region in 1965, but the most critical question never disappeared—how much real. decision-making power do local residents actually have over their political, religious, and cultural lives? We must avoid a simplistic narrative here, such as attributing decades of complex conflict to a single document or event, but we also cannot assume that the mere establishment of an autonomous region automatically puts previous controversies to rest. Because what truly makes an autonomous system function is never just a name, but rather the ability to handle disagreements between the central and local levels through institutional means , rather than simply relying on who. holds more power. After so many years of institutional arrangements, what issues in the daily lives of Tibetans today best reveal the true nature of this autonomy? I would like to start with a child and a monastery. Imagine a Tibetan child who grows up speaking the language at home, with parents telling family stories in Tibetan, but once they enter school, the main curriculum relies increasingly on Mandarin. They learn to communicate with people from other regions, but may gradually. lose the ability to read and understand history in their mother tongue. This is not to say that this happens in every Tibetan household, but in May 2020 , Human Rights Watch published a study analyzing preschool education policies in Tibetan areas and the potential impact of Mandarin becoming the primary language of instruction on the transmission of the Tibetan language. The report uses research on official documents and limited interviews; while it cannot represent every family, it highlights risks that are worth tracking . I want to be clear: there is nothing. wrong with learning Mandarin. A common language helps with education, work, and communication between different ethnic groups, but the question is: why must learning Mandarin compete with preserving the Tibetan language? Take the example of Taiwan: if one day Taiwanese, Hakka, and Indigenous languages were restricted to very little class time, and the government said, " It doesn't matter, just speak them at home." Would we worry that the next generation would become increasingly unable to read or write their mother tongue? Because language is more than just speech; it contains stories,.

classic songs, and the ways our ancestors understood the world. Culture is not just items on display in a museum ; it requires living people to continue using it. Next, let’s look at religion. For many Tibetans, Tibetan Buddhism is not just a faith, but a part of their culture, philosophy, and community life . Willingness to comply with laws and public safety regulations is certainly reasonable, but how is religious education to be passed down? To what extent should the government be allowed to intervene? This question has sparked a new debate following the "Law on. Promoting National Unity and Progress" implemented by the CCP in July 2026. Article 15 mandates that schools use the national common language and script as the basic medium for education, while also pledging to respect and protect the learning and use of minority languages. Article 46 requires religious groups, institutions, and venues to promote the shared consciousness of the Chinese nation and adhere to the Sinicization of religion. What surprises me most, however, is not these two articles, but Article 20,. which explicitly mandates that parents or other guardians must guide minors to love the Communist Party of China, the motherland, the people, and the Chinese nation, and must not instill ideas detrimental to ethnic unity and progress . Think about it: the government asking you not to discriminate against other ethnic groups is understandable, but requiring parents to guide children to love a ruling party—is that the same thing as ensuring equality? Of course, we cannot conclude that any family discussing a different history. will necessarily be punished just because this law exists; we still have to look at the actual implementation and specific cases. But if people cannot predict whether peacefully discussing ethnic history or autonomy will be interpreted as detrimental to national unity, it easily creates a pressure that discourages them from speaking out. I also want to remind everyone that when discussing these laws, we must distinguish three layers: the text of the law itself is the first, how the government actually enforces it is the second, and the impact it has on. children, families, or religious communities is the third. We cannot judge every family's experience solely based on the text of a law, nor can we ignore the actual outcomes just by looking at the official stated intentions. From the official perspective, promoting a common language and emphasizing national identity is intended to foster communication and reduce differences, and the government also highlights achievements in Tibet's infrastructure, healthcare, education, and economy— these results should be evaluated fairly based on concrete data. However, I want. to separate two things: the government helping to build schools is a public construction project, but whether you can participate in deciding how schools teach is a matter of autonomy. No matter how well-paved the roads are, they do not automatically answer the question of whether the people have a political choice. So, as we look from the 1946 Constitution and the 1951 Agreement to the new laws of 2026, we find the same question recurring: is the state protecting the coexistence of different cultures, or is it demanding that different cultures converge into a single political identity? Must the future of Tibet be a choice between only two options: independence or accepting the current system? In fact, the Dalai Lama once proposed a different political approach. Many people, upon hearing about the Tibet issue, assume it must be a choice between independence or unification. However, the "Middle Way" proposed by the 14th Dalai Lama does not set independence as the goal; instead, it advocates for genuine autonomy within the framework of the People's Republic of China through peaceful negotiation.

This proposal hopes that Tibetans can enjoy greater autonomy in matters such as culture, religion, education, and environmental protection. Local legislation and administration should also have mechanisms for democratic election, while national defense and foreign affairs remain the responsibility of the central government . This does not mean all Tibetans agree with this plan; some support genuine autonomy, while others advocate for independence. The CCP authorities also have their own opposition to the "Middle Way" and have not accepted this set of arrangements,. so we cannot package it as a universally agreed-upon answer. What is truly worth noting is that it turns abstract political disagreements into institutional issues that can be discussed concretely, such as who decides on education and how the local autonomous assemblies are formed. Under legal protection, how much autonomy is there exactly? When there is a conflict between the central government and the local region, is it decided by an independent court, or is it ultimately determined by political power? Sometimes the most difficult part of a political dispute is not that someone is being unreasonable, but that. both sides may have completely different understandings of history and sovereignty. If you demand that the other side first acknowledge your entire historical view before discussing institutions, then I fear negotiations will never proceed. But if we start with what rights and procedures are needed to live together, at least we can identify the specific content that needs to be negotiated. Of course, this does not mean that talking only about education and culture can avoid all sovereignty disputes, nor does it mean we can decide the future for Tibetans without asking for their own will. The most basic prerequisite for genuine autonomy is giving the people involved the right to participate in the choice, and this brings us to the final question : if China were to democratize in the future, would the autonomy of Tibet be guaranteed? Over the years, I have participated in many discussions on China's democratization. People discuss whether to adopt a presidential, parliamentary, or federal system in the future, and some even suggest re-examining the 1946 Constitution of the Republic of China. But I often wonder, even if the mainland. were to hold free elections one day, would the Tibet issue be automatically resolved? Suppose there is a democratically elected parliament in a future China, and the majority passes a law requiring every region to use the exact same language and education system, but Tibetans feel this impacts their culture . In that case, can the majority simply say, "We have more votes, so you must comply"? I believe it cannot be that simple, because democracy is not just about majority rule; it must also protect the fundamental rights of minorities. If ninety percent of people. vote to restrict a certain religion, does that restriction automatically conform to human rights protections? Of course not. Therefore, a constitution should not only grant the government legitimate authority but also tell the government what it cannot do, even if it has majority support. Regarding ethnic autonomy, I believe it must answer at least a few questions: can the autonomous region's assembly and government be truly elected by the local residents? How much governing authority exists over education, culture, and local affairs? Can the central. government unilaterally take that authority back? When disputes arise, can the people seek relief through an independent judicial mechanism? At the same time, autonomy cannot become a privilege for a single ethnic group; Tibet is not just inhabited by one group , but also by other residents. Guaranteeing one group's cultural and political participation does not mean that the basic rights of other ethnicities or individuals can be ignored. This is why I keep emphasizing constitutionalism, rather than just elections. The spirit of constitutionalism is to allow different groups to live under a system where power is limited, preventing whoever has the majority.

today from deciding the fate of others tomorrow. However, no matter how well a system is designed, it may not function well if the people do not understand it. Will local assembly members actually audit the budget? Do the people know how to oversee the government? When disputes occur between different ethnic groups, is everyone willing to resolve them through legal and democratic procedures? This is why I have dedicated myself to distributing civic textbooks; I hope that people don't just learn to shout about democracy, but understand how power, the rule of law, and public participation. actually work. Of course, there is another easily overlooked issue: some people may identify as Tibetan while also being willing to participate in a larger political community, while others may have completely different thoughts. These identities may not necessarily be covered by a single standard answer; a truly capable system does not need to dictate thoughts for everyone beforehand , yet can still protect each other's rights. When we re-examine Article 120 of the 1946 Constitution, we become clearer about its value and its limitations. It left behind constitutional principles worth studying, but true autonomy still requires democratic participation, specific legal protections, and a willingness to negotiate. Returning to the question at the very beginning: Tibet is named an autonomous region, so why do some still demand true autonomy? Because autonomy is not just a sign hung on a wall, nor is it whatever the government says it is. True autonomy means giving local people the right to participate in their own public affairs , such that even if the central government disagrees, these rights remain protected by the constitution and. the law. The 1946 Constitution of the Republic of China stated: "The system of self-government in Tibet shall be safeguarded." The 17-Point Agreement of 1951 also once promised autonomy, but history tells us that without a system for real implementation, even the most beautiful political promises can end up as just a piece of paper. This reminds me of the Three Principles of the People and the core political ideals of the National Revolution proposed by Dr. Sun Yat-sen back then. Nationalism should not be about demanding that all ethnic groups abandon their own cultures and identities, but about allowing different. peoples to build a political community together based on equality, freedom, and mutual respect. The Principle of Democracy is certainly not about letting a small group of power-holders decide the fate of the people, but about enabling the people to truly participate in politics, oversee the government, and have systems that safeguard their rights . As for the Principle of the People's Livelihood, it reminds us that the ultimate purpose of any political system is to ensure that every one of us can live a life with dignity and security. Therefore, I have always believed that the true meaning of the National Revolution was never just to overthrow a. regime, but more importantly, to build a nation that is free, equal, democratic, and where power is constrained by a constitution. If mainland China ever undergoes a democratic transition, we cannot simply replace one authoritarian government with another; instead, we must allow people of different ethnic groups to truly become masters of their own destiny. This is why I believe the Three Principles of the People and the constitutional democracy of the Republic of China remain worthy of our continued study, practice, and pursuit today.
